medicines.name: Estradiol patches
medicines.forms: Transdermal patch. Estradot 25, 37.5, 50, 75 and 100 micrograms per 24 hours; Estraderm MX 25, 50, 75 and 100 micrograms per 24 hours
medicines.summary: A small adhesive patch that releases estradiol through the skin, changed twice a week. It is one of the three registered ways of taking oestrogen in Australia, alongside tablets and gel.

body: Estradiol is the oestrogen used in feminising hormone therapy in Australia. It is chemically identical to the estradiol a body makes naturally, so it acts on the body the same way the body's own hormone does [1][2].

It works by binding to oestrogen receptors in breast or chest tissue, skin, bone, blood vessels and the brain, switching on the changes associated with feminisation as exposure continues over months to years [2][3].

A patch delivers it through the skin directly into the bloodstream, so it bypasses the liver on first pass. Australian guidance prefers patches and gel over tablets because the transdermal route does not raise clotting factors the way swallowed oestrogen does, so the risk of a blood clot is lower — this matters most for people over 40, people who smoke, or anyone who already carries other clot risk factors [1][4].

Two brands are registered here: Estradot, in five strengths, and Estraderm MX, in four [2][3]. The two are not automatically interchangeable milligram-for-milligram at every strength, so check with a pharmacist before swapping brands rather than assuming they match.

Before starting, a prescriber should take a general medical and family history. Oestrogen reduces sperm production over time, so fertility and sperm cryopreservation are worth discussing before the first dose if having biological children later matters to you [1][2].
list: Estradot — 25, 37.5, 50, 75 and 100 micrograms per 24 hours [2]
Estraderm MX — 25, 50, 75 and 100 micrograms per 24 hours [3]

body: Both brands are changed twice a week. The Estradot leaflet puts it as "You will apply a new patch twice weekly (every 3 or 4 days)" [2]; Estraderm MX patches are "replaced every 3-4 days" [3]. Most people pick two fixed days and keep to them, such as Monday and Thursday.

The two brands approve different skin sites, so follow the leaflet for the brand you actually have. Estradot goes on "a clean, dry area of the abdomen" [2]. For Estraderm MX, "the best place to apply ESTRADERM MX patches is on your lower abdomen or buttocks. Never put ESTRADERM MX patches on your breasts" [3].

Leave the patch in its pouch until you are ready to use it, and change the spot each time rather than using the same patch of skin twice in a row [2][3]. Neither brand's patch should be cut or torn to change the dose — "the patch must not be cut or torn" — because that changes how much estradiol is released [2][3].

Bathing, showering and swimming are fine with a patch on. For Estraderm MX, "the patch might, however, become detached from the skin in very hot water or in the sauna" [3]. Keep the patch out of direct sunlight and off a solarium, since heat and UV can affect how much hormone it releases [2][3].

If a patch falls off before its scheduled change, both leaflets say to deal with it straight away rather than wait: Estradot's advice is that "the same patch may be reapplied. If necessary, a new patch may be applied. In either case, the original treatment schedule should be continued" [2]. Estraderm MX's advice is to "put a new patch on for the rest of the 3-4 days" [3]. Either way, keep the same two weekly change days going forward rather than resetting the schedule from the day it fell off.
list: Clean, dry, unbroken skin — not over breast or chest tissue [2][3]
Avoid the waistline, where a belt or waistband rubs the patch loose
Press the patch down firmly and run a finger around the edges
Rotate the site every change [2][3]
Do not cut, trim or fold the patch to adjust the dose [2][3]
Keep it out of direct sunlight, a solarium, and very hot water or saunas where possible [2][3]
sections.note: If a patch falls off early, or will not stick on you at all, that is worth telling your prescriber or pharmacist — adhesive performance genuinely differs between brands and between people.

body: The Australian position statement describes starting at a lower strength and building up, with a usual maintenance range of 100 to 150 micrograms per 24 hours. At the upper end that can mean wearing more than one patch at a time [1].

The Equinox prescribing guide groups transdermal doses as low (25–50 micrograms), medium (50–100 micrograms) and high (75–100 micrograms), and treats products within the same dose band as roughly equivalent when switching brands [4].

Dose is usually reviewed and adjusted no sooner than six to eight weeks after a change, since blood levels take time to settle at a new steady state and changing too soon makes the blood test hard to interpret [1][4].
If an anti-androgen or a GnRH analogue is also prescribed, less estradiol may be needed to reach the same blood level, because there is less endogenous testosterone to counter [1][4].
Some people, including many non-binary people, deliberately aim for partial changes on a lower dose. That is a recognised and legitimate goal to raise with a prescriber [1].
list: Typical starting range — around 25 to 50 micrograms per 24 hours [1][4]
Usual maintenance range described in the position statement — 100 to 150 micrograms per 24 hours [1]
Changed twice a week, every three or four days [2][3]
Dose changes reviewed with a blood test no sooner than six to eight weeks later [1][4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Most of these settle as the body adjusts, and many are the intended effects of oestrogen rather than problems. The position statement notes that "most effects begin within a few months but maximal effects may take two to three years" to fully develop [1].
Skin irritation under the patch is the commonest complaint that is specific to this form [2][3].

Changes to sexual function are expected and usually intended: reduced spontaneous erections and a lower sex drive are common as testosterone falls, alongside a gradual fall in testicular volume and sperm production [1].
list: Irritation, redness or itch where the patch sits [2][3]
Breast or chest tenderness, and breast or chest growth [2][3]
Headache, nausea or dizziness [2][3]
Fluid retention in the legs or ankles [2][3]
Mood changes, and changes in weight [2]
Softer skin, redistribution of body fat, decreased muscle mass [1]
Reduced libido, fewer spontaneous erections, smaller testicular volume, reduced sperm production [1]

body: The Estradot leaflet is direct about this: "Call your doctor straight away, or go straight to the Emergency Department at your nearest hospital if you notice any of these serious side effects" [2].
The signs below are mostly about blood clots, the liver, or an allergic reaction. They are uncommon, but they are the reason the leaflet says emergency department rather than next appointment.

Both leaflets list specific reasons treatment should be stopped and reviewed rather than continued: "an increase in epileptic seizures, jaundice or deterioration in liver function, a significant increase in blood pressure, new onset of migraine type headache, pregnancy" [2][3].

Taking too much oestrogen from a patch is unlikely, since the skin limits how fast it is absorbed. If it happens, "the effects of overdosage can be rapidly reversed by removal of the patch," and symptoms are usually limited to breast tenderness or unexpected bleeding [2]. The Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) can advise on any suspected overdose.
list: Sudden shortness of breath, coughing up blood, chest pain, or fainting — possible clot in the lung [2][3]
Unusual pain, heat or swelling in an arm or leg — possible clot in a vein [2][3]
Symptoms of a stroke or heart attack, including sudden weakness, slurred speech or crushing chest pain [2]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2][3]
Severe abdominal pain with fever [2]
Rash, or swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing [2][3]
New migraine-type headache, a marked rise in blood pressure, or increased seizures if you have epilepsy — reasons to stop and review, not necessarily an emergency department visit [2][3]
sections.note: Do not wait for a GP appointment for chest pain, breathing difficulty, stroke symptoms or a severe allergic reaction. Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department.

body: Blood tests here are not a pass or fail. They tell your prescriber whether the dose is doing what you both want.

Australian guidance suggests a trough oestradiol of about 250 to 600 pmol/L with total testosterone below 2 nmol/L, rechecked six to eight weeks after any dose change rather than straight away [1][4].

"Trough" means the blood is drawn just before the next patch change, when the level is at its lowest point of the cycle — taking it straight after a fresh patch goes on overstates the dose being delivered.

Some anticonvulsants, rifampicin-type antibiotics, certain HIV medicines and St John's wort can speed up how the liver clears oestrogen and lower the blood level on the same dose — mention any new prescription or supplement to whoever is monitoring your bloods [2][3].
list: Oestradiol and total testosterone [1][4]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1]
Reviews roughly every three months through the first year, then every six to twelve months [1]
Screening follows the organs you have, not your gender — chest or breast tissue, and prostate tissue, which genital surgery does not remove [1]

body: Estradot: "Store it in a cool dry place", away from the bathroom, the car and window sills [2]. The CMI also specifies storing below 25°C, protected from light, and not frozen [2].
Estraderm MX: "Keep your patches in a cool dry place below 25°C", and keep each patch in its protective pouch until you are ready to apply it [3].

For a used patch, fold it in half with the sticky side inwards before throwing it away, so the remaining hormone in the patch is not left exposed — a used patch still contains a substantial amount of active estradiol [2].

Keep patches out of reach of children and pets, since accidental contact can deliver an unintended dose. Ask your pharmacist how to get rid of used patches and anything you no longer need — any pharmacy can take unwanted medicines back [3].
Estradiol patches are PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restriction attached, so any prescriber can write them and no authority is needed. You pay the standard co-payment [5].

Estradot is listed at 25, 37.5, 50, 75 and 100 micrograms per 24 hours (items 8761D, 8762E, 8763F, 8764G and 8765H). Estraderm MX is listed at 25, 50 and 100 micrograms per 24 hours (items 8311K, 8140K and 8312L) [5].

The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70. Once a household's PBS spending reaches the safety net threshold for the calendar year — $1,748.20 for general patients, $277.20 for concession card holders — remaining scripts cost less or nothing for the rest of that year [8].
If a substitute or imported product is supplied during a shortage, ask your pharmacist whether that specific product is subsidised, because not all of them are [6].

Estradiol patches have been the long-running shortage in Australian gender-affirming care. The TGA lists Estradot 25, 50, 75 and 100 micrograms as in shortage with supply expected to return by 31 December 2026. Estradot 37.5 micrograms is recorded as resolved [6].
For Estraderm MX, the TGA records the 25 and 75 microgram strengths as resolved, and gave 31 August 2026 as the expected return for the 50 and 100 microgram strengths [6].

A Serious Scarcity Substitution Instrument is in force, which lets a pharmacist supply an alternative brand of estradiol patch at the same strength, or two half-strength patches adding up to the same daily amount, without a new prescription. The instrument runs to 28 February 2027 [6][7].

A pharmacist using the instrument must get informed consent before substituting — explaining the brand difference, including how the adhesive and application method differ — and must tell the prescriber by phone, fax or email as soon as practical afterwards [7].

Raise it with your pharmacist before you run out, not on your last day of supply. If no patch brand or strength combination is available at all, that is a conversation for your prescriber about an interim tablet or gel dose rather than going without.

medicines.name: Estradiol tablets
medicines.forms: Oral tablet. Progynova 1 mg and 2 mg estradiol valerate; Zumenon 2 mg estradiol
medicines.summary: A daily tablet that supplies estradiol by mouth. It is the cheapest and simplest oestrogen to take, and the form Australian guidance is most cautious about where the risk of blood clots is raised.

body: Estradiol is the oestrogen used in feminising hormone therapy in Australia — the same hormone a body makes naturally, given as a medicine [1]. It works by binding to oestrogen receptors in breast or chest tissue, skin, bone and the brain, driving feminising changes as exposure continues over months to years [1].

Two registered brands are used. Progynova contains estradiol valerate, in 1 mg and 2 mg tablets [2]. Zumenon contains "2 mg of estradiol (as hemihydrate)" [3]. The body converts estradiol valerate to estradiol, so in practice they do the same job.
Ethinylestradiol, the oestrogen in the combined contraceptive pill, is not used for gender affirmation. The high doses used here until 1989 were linked to more blood clots [1].

Tablets pass through the liver before reaching the rest of the body. Because of that, Australian guidance prefers patches or gel where the risk of clotting is higher, such as over the age of 40, in smokers, or with other clot risk factors [1].

Before starting, oestrogen's effect on fertility is worth discussing — sperm production falls over time on oestrogen, so sperm cryopreservation is worth raising with a prescriber beforehand if having biological children later matters to you [1].

One tablet, by mouth, at about the same time each day. Progynova: "Take one tablet at the same time each day. Swallow the tablets whole with a glass of water" [2]. Zumenon: "The usual dose is one tablet daily", taken at about the same time each day [3]. Food does not change how much is absorbed, so it can be taken with or without a meal [2].
Australian practice often splits the daily amount into two doses across the day rather than taking it all at once [1][4].
Some prescribers ask for tablets to be taken under the tongue instead of swallowed. That changes how the medicine is absorbed, so only do it if your prescriber has specifically told you to [5].

If a dose is missed, the two brands' leaflets give slightly different windows, but the principle is the same: catch up promptly if you remember the same day, otherwise skip it and carry on — never double up. Progynova's leaflet says that within 24 hours, "take your tablet as soon as possible, and take the next one at the normal time," but warns that "if you miss tablets for several days, irregular bleeding may occur" [2]. Zumenon's leaflet is more precise: "if it is less than 12 hours before your next dose, skip the dose you missed"; otherwise "take it as soon as you remember, and then go back to taking your medicine as you would normally" — and either way, "do not take a double dose to make up for the dose that you missed" [3].
The Progynova leaflet also flags that heavy alcohol use "has an influence on the treatment" — worth mentioning to your prescriber if your drinking changes [2].
The usual range in Australian guidance is 2 to 6 mg daily, often split into two doses, and sometimes titrated up to 8 mg [1][4].
A lower dose aiming at partial changes is a recognised goal, not an incomplete version of treatment [1].
Dose changes are usually reviewed with a blood test no sooner than six to eight weeks later, since levels take time to settle and testing too soon is hard to interpret [1][4].

Zumenon's leaflet advises stopping "at least four weeks before elective surgery" that carries a raised risk of blood clots, and restarting only once you are fully mobile again afterwards — this is worth planning with both your prescriber and your surgical team well ahead of any operation [3].
list: Usual range — 2 to 6 mg daily, often in two doses [1][4]
Sometimes titrated to 8 mg daily [1]
Levels rechecked six to eight weeks after a change [1][4]
Stopped around four weeks before surgery carrying a clot risk, on current CMI advice [3]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Many of these are the intended effects of oestrogen, and several settle after the first few months. The Zumenon leaflet notes that "nausea, headache and oedema may occur but symptoms are normally transient" [3].
The position statement notes that "most effects begin within a few months but maximal effects may take two to three years" to fully develop [1].
list: Breast or chest tenderness, and breast or chest growth [2][3]
Nausea or indigestion [2][3]
Headache, migraine or dizziness [2]
Swelling in the hands, ankles or feet [3]
Mood changes [2]
Reduced libido, fewer spontaneous erections, smaller testicular volume, reduced sperm production, over time [1]

body: Seek medical help immediately — emergency department or 000, not a routine appointment — for any of the following, which the leaflets flag as serious [2][3].

Both leaflets also list reasons to stop taking the tablet straight away and contact your prescriber, even without going to hospital: a first migraine attack or worsening migraines, severe headaches, sudden changes in vision or hearing, whole-body itching, unexplained upper abdominal pain, jaundice, a marked rise in blood pressure, or finding out you are pregnant [2][3].

Taking too much is uncommon but possible with tablets, unlike a patch. "If you think that you have used too much PROGYNOVA®, you may need urgent medical attention" — there is no specific antidote, so treatment in hospital is aimed at the symptoms, mainly nausea and vomiting [2]. Call the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) for advice on any suspected overdose.
list: Sudden shortness of breath, coughing up blood, chest pain or fainting [2][3]
Unusual pain or swelling in an arm or leg [2][3]
Sudden loss of vision, or a new migraine-type headache you have not had before [3]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [3]
Severe abdominal pain with fever [3]
Irregular heartbeat [2]
"Signs of allergy such as rash, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, throat" [2]
sections.note: Blood clots are the reason this list matters most for tablets. If you cannot decide whether something counts, treat it as though it does and get it checked.

body: Australian guidance suggests a trough oestradiol of about 250 to 600 pmol/L with total testosterone below 2 nmol/L, rechecked six to eight weeks after a dose change [1][4].
Reviews also cover blood pressure, weight, smoking, and how you are going in yourself [1].

A number of medicines and supplements can lower the oestradiol level a tablet dose achieves by speeding up how the liver clears it, including some anticonvulsants, rifampicin, certain antivirals and St John's wort — mention any new prescription or supplement to whoever monitors your bloods [2][3].
list: Oestradiol and total testosterone [1][4]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1]
Glucose or HbA1c and lipids periodically, particularly with other risk factors [1]
Screening based on the organs you have, including chest or breast tissue and prostate tissue [1]

body: Progynova storage differs by strength: "PROGYNOVA® 1 mg: Store below 30°C" and "PROGYNOVA® 2 mg: Store below 25°C" [2].
Zumenon: "Keep the medicine in a cool, dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C" [3].
Both leaflets say to avoid the bathroom, near a sink, the car and window sills, and to keep tablets out of reach of children [2][3]. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Both brands are PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restriction, so no authority is needed and the standard co-payment applies [6].
Progynova is listed as estradiol valerate 1 mg (item 1663M) and 2 mg (item 1664N) in packs of 56. Zumenon is listed as estradiol 2 mg, 56 tablets (item 8274L) [6].

The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70. Once a household's PBS spending reaches the safety net threshold for the year — $1,748.20 for general patients, $277.20 for concession card holders — remaining scripts cost less or nothing for the rest of the calendar year [8].
The TGA has published a substitution instrument specifically for Progynova, across multiple strengths, which confirms a real shortage history for this brand [7].
Whether that instrument is still in force today is worth checking rather than assuming — ask your pharmacist, who can see the current position, or check the TGA page directly.
No current Australian shortage record was located for Zumenon.

Because tablets are cheap, simple to store and rarely in short supply compared with patches, some prescribers use a short course of tablets as a bridge when a preferred patch or gel brand is temporarily unavailable — raise that option with your prescriber rather than going without oestrogen altogether.

medicines.name: Estradiol gel
medicines.forms: Transdermal gel. Sandrena 0.1% in 0.5 g and 1 g sachets (0.5 mg and 1 mg estradiol); Estrogel 0.06% pump, 0.75 mg estradiol per 1.25 g actuation
medicines.summary: A clear gel rubbed into the skin once a day. Like a patch, it delivers estradiol without passing through the liver first, and it suits people who want a daily routine or small dose steps rather than an adhesive.

body: Estradiol gel is the same hormone as the tablets and patches, in a gel that dries on the skin. It works by binding to oestrogen receptors in breast or chest tissue, skin, bone and the brain, and because it is absorbed through the skin it avoids the first pass through the liver — Australian guidance groups it with patches as preferred where clot risk is higher [1].

Two registered products are used here, and they are measured differently. Sandrena comes as single-use sachets — "0.5 g or 1 g sachets" containing 0.5 mg or 1 mg of estradiol [2]. Estrogel comes as a metered pump, where "each 1.25g dose of Estrogel gel contains 0.75 mg of estradiol (as hemihydrate)" [3].
Because the two are dosed in different units, do not convert between them yourself. Your prescriber will write the one you are being supplied.

Before starting, oestrogen's effect on fertility is worth discussing — sperm production falls over time on oestrogen, so sperm cryopreservation is worth raising with a prescriber beforehand if having biological children later matters to you [1].
Once a day, at about the same time, on clean dry skin.

The approved sites differ. For Sandrena, "apply the gel to your lower body or thighs" and "alternate the application site each day" — not on breast or chest tissue, the face, or irritated skin [2]. For Estrogel, spread it over a large area of the outer arms, shoulders or mid-inner thighs, and not near breast or chest tissue or the genitals [3].

Let it dry before dressing. Sandrena says to "allow the gel to dry for a few minutes" and "do not wash the area where you have applied the gel for at least one hour" [2]. Estrogel says "leave to dry for 5 minutes before covering with clothes," and separately warns not to "wash the skin or apply other skin care products until at least one hour after application" — that includes strong cleansers and alcohol-based skincare, which can change how much is absorbed [3].
Wash your hands afterwards. Estrogel: "wash hands with soap and water after applying the gel" [3].

If a dose is missed, both brands use the same 12-hour rule: apply it as soon as you remember if you are within 12 hours of the missed time, otherwise skip it and apply the next dose as usual — never double up [2][3]. Both leaflets warn that missed doses can cause unexpected spotting or bleeding [2][3].
If you tend to get patchy skin darkening (chloasma) with oestrogen, Sandrena's leaflet specifically advises minimising sun or UV exposure while using it [2].
list: One sachet, or the number of pump presses your prescriber has set [2][3]
Rotate the site day to day [2]
Let it dry, then cover with clothing [2][3]
Wash your hands straight after [2][3]
Do not wash the area or apply other skin products there for at least an hour [2][3]
If more than 12 hours late, skip that dose rather than doubling up [2][3]
sections.note: Sandrena carries a specific safety instruction about transfer, quoted from the leaflet: "Cover the application area with clothing as soon as the gel has dried to prevent accidental transfer of the gel to others (e.g., child or spouse or pet)" [2].

body: Sandrena: "The usual starting dose is one 0.5 g or 1 g sachet per day" [2].
For the pump, the Equinox prescribing guide describes one to three pumps daily, each delivering 0.75 mg of estradiol [4], which matches the Estrogel leaflet's stated 0.75 mg per 1.25 g actuation [3].
Dose changes are usually reviewed with a blood test no sooner than six to eight weeks later, since levels take time to settle at a new steady state [1][4].
list: Sandrena — usually one 0.5 g or 1 g sachet daily [2]
Pump gel — one to three pumps daily, 0.75 mg estradiol per pump [3][4]
Levels rechecked six to eight weeks after a change [1][4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Most are the same as for other forms of oestrogen. Skin reactions at the application site are the one specific to gel.
The position statement notes that "most effects begin within a few months but maximal effects may take two to three years" to fully develop [1].
list: Breast or chest pain or tenderness [2][3]
Headache [2][3]
Nausea, or stomach cramps [2]
Tiredness [2]
Weight changes and mood swings [3]
Vaginal discharge, in people who have a vagina [2][3]
Reduced libido, fewer spontaneous erections, smaller testicular volume, reduced sperm production, over time [1]

body: Get urgent medical help — emergency department or 000 — for any of these. Both leaflets treat them as needing immediate care [2][3].

Both leaflets also list reasons to stop the gel and contact your prescriber even without an emergency: jaundice or worsening liver function, a significant rise in blood pressure, a new migraine-type headache, or finding out you are pregnant [2][3].

Genuine overdose from gel is unlikely because the skin limits absorption. Symptoms, if they occur, are usually breast tenderness, nausea or unexpected bleeding, and settle once the dose is reduced or stopped — call the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) for advice on any suspected overdose [2][3].
list: Painful swelling in a leg, or sudden chest pain — possible blood clot [2][3]
Sudden difficulty breathing [3]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2][3]
A new breast or chest lump, or unexpected bleeding from the vagina if you have one [3]
sections.note: Do not wait for your next appointment for any of the above.

body: The same blood tests as for other forms of oestrogen: trough oestradiol of about 250 to 600 pmol/L with total testosterone below 2 nmol/L in Australian guidance [1][4].

Timing matters more for gel than for most forms. Equinox describes taking the sample in the morning, before that day's dose, after at least a week of steady use [4]. A sample taken at the wrong point can look far too high or too low when nothing is wrong.
The same medicines that can lower blood oestradiol by speeding up liver clearance apply here too — certain anticonvulsants, rifampicin-type antibiotics, some HIV medicines and St John's wort [2][3].
list: Oestradiol and total testosterone, timed before the day's dose [1][4]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1]
Reviews about every three months in the first year, then every six to twelve months [1]
sections.note: Ask for the required timing to be written on your pathology form, and tell the collection centre when your last dose was.

body: Sandrena: "Store below 25°C", in a cool dry place away from moisture and heat [2].
Estrogel: "Keep your medicine in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C", and not in the bathroom, near a sink, on a window sill or in the car [3].
Keep gel out of reach of children and pets, both because of the medicine itself and because of the transfer risk. Return what you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Sandrena is PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restriction — estradiol 0.1% gel, 28 x 1 g sachets, item 8286D [5].
The PBS also lists estradiol 0.1% gel in 28 x 500 mg sachets, and estradiol 0.06% gel at 750 micrograms per actuation in a 64-actuation pack, which is the Estrogel presentation [5].
Gel listings have changed over time and not every gel product has been subsidised in every year, so confirm the current price for the specific product you are being given rather than assuming [5].

The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70. Once a household's PBS spending reaches the safety net threshold for the year — $1,748.20 general, $277.20 concessional — remaining scripts cost less or nothing for the rest of the calendar year [7].
No current TGA shortage notice was located for estradiol gel in Australia. That is not the same as a confirmed all-clear, so treat it as unconfirmed rather than guaranteed [6].

Gel has been one of the alternatives people move to during the long-running estradiol patch shortage, which can put pressure on its own supply. Your pharmacist can tell you what is actually available locally.

Because Sandrena and Estrogel are dosed in different units — sachet strength versus pump actuations — a forced switch between them because of a shortage needs your prescriber to reset the dose, not a straight substitution at the pharmacy counter.

list: What blood oestradiol level are we aiming for on my current dose, and when will you recheck it?
Should my blood test be timed before or after that day's dose, and what should I tell the collection centre?
If I switch between Sandrena and Estrogel because of stock issues, how will my dose be converted?
What's my realistic timeline for skin, breast or chest, fat distribution and libido changes on gel specifically?
How do I avoid transferring gel to a partner, child or pet, and what do I do if that happens?
Given oestrogen's effect on sperm production, do I need to think about fertility preservation before we go any higher?

medicines.name: Micronised progesterone
medicines.forms: Prometrium: soft capsules, 100 mg and 200 mg. Utrogestan: soft capsules, 200 mg, 300 mg and 400 mg, registered in Australia for vaginal use
medicines.summary: A progestogen that some people take alongside oestrogen. It is also used the other way around, to manage bleeding for people on testosterone.

body: Progesterone is a separate hormone from oestrogen. Micronised progesterone is the form most used in Australia, and Prometrium is the brand most often prescribed [1][2].

The 2019 Australian position statement is direct about adding it to feminising hormone therapy for breast or chest growth: "despite anecdotal reports that progestins increase breast growth, no data support their use," and it notes that in postmenopausal women, adding a progestin to oestrogen raised the risk of coronary heart disease compared with oestrogen alone, and can increase the risk of blood clots, bloating, nausea and weight gain — its conclusion is that progestins "are not recommended" for this purpose [1]. Despite that, some prescribers still offer it off-label because some patients report a subjective benefit; it is worth asking your own prescriber where they stand and why.

It is also used in the opposite direction. If periods continue on testosterone and cause distress, the position statement lists the options as raising the testosterone dose, an oral progestogen, or a progestogen-releasing IUD [1].

The two brands are not interchangeable in Australia. Prometrium is "progesterone 100 mg or 200 mg" in soft gelatin capsules, taken by mouth [2]. Utrogestan comes in 200 mg, 300 mg and 400 mg capsules and its Australian leaflet states that "UTROGESTAN is intended to be inserted into the vagina" [3].

Progesterone acts differently from oestrogen and testosterone: rather than driving new tissue growth, its listed pharmacological effects are described as "antiestrogenic, slightly antiandrogenic and antialdosterone" [2].
Prometrium capsules are "taken by mouth and swallowed whole with a glass of water", and the leaflet notes that food changes how the body handles the medicine [2].
It is commonly taken at night. The leaflet reports that "cases of drowsiness and dizzy sensations have been reported", and that taking the capsules at bedtime reduces this [2].

If a dose is missed, Prometrium's leaflet gives the standard rule: "if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose when you are meant to, as usual" — otherwise take it as soon as remembered, and never double up to make up for a missed dose [2].
Smoking can lower how much of the dose reaches the bloodstream, and alcohol can increase it — both are worth mentioning to your prescriber if either changes for you [2].

Utrogestan, as registered in Australia, is inserted into the vagina rather than swallowed, and its listed uses are in fertility treatment and pregnancy rather than hormone therapy [3]. If you have been given Utrogestan, follow the instructions you were given — they may differ from the leaflet's registered uses, and your prescriber can explain why.
sections.note: Prometrium "contains soya lecithin", which can trigger a reaction in people who are sensitive to soya — tell your prescriber or pharmacist if that applies to you [2].

body: The Equinox prescribing guide describes micronised progesterone 100 mg daily, usually taken at night, as the dose used alongside feminising hormone therapy [4].
list: Micronised progesterone 100 mg daily, usually at night [4]
Progesterone levels are not routinely checked [4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Most reported effects are mild and often settle. Drowsiness is the one that shapes when people take it [2].
list: Drowsiness or a dizzy sensation, which is why it is usually taken at bedtime [2]
Headache [2]
Breakthrough or irregular bleeding, in people who bleed [2]
Tiredness [2]
Weight changes and breast or chest discomfort [2]
"Mild mood changes" and disturbed sleep [2]

body: Get urgent medical help — emergency department or 000 — for any of the following. Both leaflets treat swelling of the face, mouth or throat as an emergency [2][3].

Prometrium's leaflet also lists reasons to stop and get medical advice promptly, even without going to hospital: new vision changes, jaundice, a new or severe migraine, or sudden problems with speech or coordination [2].

Overdose symptoms reported in the leaflet are drowsiness, dizziness, a feeling of euphoria, or irregular bleeding. Management is observation and supportive care rather than a specific antidote — contact the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) for advice on any suspected overdose [2].
list: Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or hives [2][3]
Chest pain, or pain and swelling in a leg — possible blood clot [2]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2]
New or severe migraine, or problems with your vision [2]
sections.note: Because it is usually taken at night, drowsiness the next morning is common and expected. Drowsiness that stops you driving or working safely is worth reporting rather than living with.

body: Progesterone levels are not routinely measured in Australian practice [4]. The monitoring around it is the monitoring for the rest of your hormone therapy.
If you are taking it to manage bleeding on testosterone, the thing being reviewed is whether the bleeding has settled — which is a conversation, not a blood test [1].

Certain epilepsy medicines, rifampicin, spironolactone, griseofulvin, some antibiotics and some antifungals can change how progesterone is broken down — mention any new prescription to your prescriber [2].
Prometrium: store "in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C. DO NOT REFRIGERATE", in the original packaging, away from bathrooms and cars, and out of reach of children [2].
Utrogestan: "Store below 30°C" in a cool dry place away from moisture, heat and sunlight [3].
Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.

Micronised progesterone 100 mg capsules are PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restrictions — progesterone 100 mg capsule, 30, item 14730G. The brands listed against that item include Prometrium, Progesterone ADVZ 100 and PROGESTERONE-APX [5].
Because several brands share the item, ask your pharmacist for one with no brand premium if cost matters.

Vaginal progesterone products, including pessaries and gel, are listed separately [5]. The Australian PBS listings for progesterone are not written for gender-affirming care specifically — the General Schedule listing means no authority is required.
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][7].
The TGA has registered an additional progesterone supplier in Australia, which is often a sign of pressure on the original brand, but no current shortage notice for Prometrium was confirmed [6].
Treat the supply position as unconfirmed rather than clear, and ask your pharmacist before you get low.

Because several brands share the same PBS item at the same strength, a pharmacist can usually substitute another progesterone 100 mg brand at the counter if Prometrium specifically is out of stock, without needing to contact your prescriber first [5].

list: Given the position statement says there is no data supporting progesterone for breast or chest growth, why are you recommending it for me specifically?
If I am taking it to manage bleeding on testosterone, how long should we trial it before trying a different option?
Is taking it at night actually necessary for me, or could a different time suit my routine better?
Do I need any extra monitoring while taking progesterone alongside my other hormones?
If my brand is unavailable, is it safe for the pharmacist to substitute another progesterone 100 mg brand automatically?
Am I a candidate for stopping progesterone altogether if it isn't giving me a benefit I can point to?

medicines.name: Cyproterone acetate
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, 50 mg and 100 mg
medicines.summary: A tablet that strongly lowers the effect of testosterone, and a progestogen in its own right. It is one of the two androgen blockers used in Australia, and the one with the most important long-term safety limit.

body: Oestrogen on its own does not usually suppress testosterone enough, so a blocker is often added. Two are used in Australia: cyproterone acetate and spironolactone. There is no good head-to-head evidence that one is better, so the choice comes down to your health history and how you tolerate it [1].

Cyproterone works in two ways at once. It "inhibits competitively the effect of androgens" directly at the tissues androgens act on, and separately it has "a progestogenic action" that reduces the release of the pituitary hormones LH and FSH, which in turn lowers how much testosterone the testes produce [2].
Cyproterone is the stronger of the two blockers, and that strength is also why its long-term dose is kept as low as possible [1].

Australian brands include Androcur 50 mg tablets, Androcur-100, Anterone and Cyproterone Sandoz [5]. Cyprostat has been permanently withdrawn by its sponsor and its ARTG registration cancelled — that is a discontinuation, not a temporary shortage, so anyone who was on Cyprostat needs a different brand [6].
A tablet by mouth, once a day or on set days of the week, as your prescriber directs.
Australian guidance is explicit about using the lowest effective dose, because the main long-term risk rises with the total amount taken over the years [1][3].
Once testosterone is suppressed, some prescribers reduce the frequency rather than stopping altogether [3].

If a dose is missed, the standard advice applies: "if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose when you are meant to"; otherwise take it as soon as remembered, and never double up [2].

Alcohol can blunt how well cyproterone works: "alcohol may prevent Androcur from working as well as it should in reducing abnormal sex drive," and it can also worsen the tiredness and concentration problems the tablet can cause on its own [2].
After an orchidectomy a blocker is no longer needed and is usually stopped [1].
Typical Australian doses are 12.5 to 25 mg daily — well below the doses this medicine was originally registered for [1][3].
Some prescribers reduce further, to 12.5 mg two or three times a week, once testosterone is suppressed [3].
list: Typical range — 12.5 to 25 mg daily [1][3]
Reduced maintenance — 12.5 mg two or three times a week for some people [3]
Lowest effective dose is the explicit goal, because the risk of meningioma rises with cumulative dose [1][2]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: The commonest reported effects are tiredness, weight change, headache, low mood, nausea and reduced sex drive [2].
Reduced sex drive and fewer spontaneous erections are expected effects of blocking testosterone rather than side effects in the usual sense, but they can still be distressing and are worth raising.
list: Tiredness [2]
Weight changes [2]
Headache [2]
Low or depressed mood [2]
Nausea [2]
Reduced sex drive, and reduced erections for people who have them [2]
Breast or chest tenderness [2]

body: The Androcur leaflet says: "Call your doctor straight away, or go straight to the Emergency Department at your nearest hospital if you notice any of these serious side effects" [2].

Two specific risks shape how this medicine is prescribed and monitored in Australia. The first is meningioma — a tumour of the lining of the brain, usually not cancerous but still serious. The Australian product information reports it with long-term use at doses of 25 mg a day and above, with the risk rising as the total dose taken over the years adds up. If a meningioma is diagnosed, cyproterone must be stopped permanently [1][2].

The second is the liver. Direct liver toxicity, including jaundice, hepatitis and liver failure, has been reported, particularly at doses of 100 mg a day and above [2]. Prolactinoma, a benign pituitary tumour, has also been reported [1].

Taking too much is uncommon but the leaflet is clear about what to do: "if you think that you have used too much Androcur, you may need urgent medical attention" — no specific antidote exists, so call the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) or go to the emergency department [2].
list: Yellowing of the skin or eyes, pale bowel motions, or dark urine — liver injury [2]
Sudden severe headache, loss of vision, loss of coordination or slurred speech [2]
Shortness of breath or chest pain [2]
Persistent new headaches, changes in vision, hearing changes or seizures — raise these promptly, as they can be symptoms of a meningioma [1][2]
sections.note: For sudden severe headache, vision loss, slurred speech, chest pain or breathlessness, call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department. Do not wait.

body: Liver function blood tests are the specific extra check for cyproterone. The Australian product information advises testing before treatment, regularly during treatment, and whenever symptoms suggest liver injury [2][3].
Red blood cell counts and adrenal function are also monitored during treatment [2].
Alongside that, the usual feminising-therapy monitoring applies: trough oestradiol of about 250 to 600 pmol/L and total testosterone below 2 nmol/L in Australian guidance [1][3].

Several medicines can raise cyproterone levels by slowing its breakdown, including some antifungals (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clotrimazole) and ritonavir; others, including phenytoin, rifampicin and St John's wort, can lower its level and reduce how well it works — tell whoever monitors your bloods about any new prescription or supplement [2].
list: Liver function tests before and during treatment [2][3]
Full blood count, and adrenal function [2]
Oestradiol and total testosterone [1][3]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1]
New or persistent headaches and vision changes reported promptly, because of meningioma risk [1][2]

body: Store below 30°C in a cool dry place, away from the bathroom, near a sink and window sills, and keep tablets in their original packaging until you take them [2].
Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Cyproterone acetate 50 mg tablets are PBS-listed as a Restricted Benefit — item 14023C, cyproterone acetate 50 mg tablet, 50 [5]. No authority is needed.

The restriction is about quantity, not about who may have the medicine. The wording is: "The condition must be stable for the prescriber to consider the listed maximum quantity of this medicine suitable for this patient" [5].

Several brands share that item. Anterone 50 and Cyproterone Sandoz are benchmark-priced; Androcur carries a brand premium of about $4.00 on the 50 mg pack, which you pay on top of your co-payment and which does not count towards the Safety Net [5]. Ask your pharmacist for a brand with no premium if cost matters.
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][8].
Androcur's ARTG registrations remain active and no current shortage notice was located for it [4][7].

Cyprostat is a different matter: it was cancelled at the sponsor's request under Section 30(1)(c) of the Therapeutic Goods Act and is not coming back [6]. If you were previously on Cyprostat, your prescriber needs to move you to Androcur, Androcur-100, Anterone or Cyproterone Sandoz — the dose does not necessarily convert one-for-one between brands, so this is not a simple pharmacy swap.
Because several brands of cyproterone are registered here, a shortage of one is usually covered by another. Your pharmacist can swap brands of the same strength.

list: Given the meningioma risk rises with cumulative dose, could I move to a lower or less frequent dose now that my testosterone is suppressed?
How often will my liver function be checked, and what result would make you stop the medicine?
Should I be alert to any particular headache or vision symptom given my current dose and how long I've been on it?
Would spironolactone suit me better, given my own health history?
Since Cyprostat has been discontinued, which brand am I actually on now, and does the strength match what I was taking before?
If I have surgery planned, does cyproterone need to be stopped beforehand?

medicines.name: Spironolactone
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, 25 mg and 100 mg
medicines.summary: A tablet that blocks the effect of testosterone and also acts as a mild diuretic. It is the gentler of the two androgen blockers used in Australia, and the one that needs kidney and potassium checks.

body: Spironolactone was developed as a diuretic — a medicine that makes the kidneys pass more water and salt — and it works against a hormone called aldosterone, which is why it holds onto potassium while flushing out fluid [1][2]. It also blocks androgen receptors directly, giving it an "anti-androgenic effect" against testosterone, which is why it is used as a blocker in feminising therapy [2].

It is one of the two blockers used in Australia. There is no good head-to-head evidence that spironolactone or cyproterone is better, so the choice comes down to your health history and how you tolerate it [1].
Registered brands here are Spiractin, Aldactone and Spironolactone Viatris, in 25 mg and 100 mg tablets [2][3].
A tablet by mouth, once or twice a day as your prescriber directs, "with or immediately after food" [2].

Because it is a diuretic, it can make you pass more urine, particularly at first. Some people prefer to take the later dose earlier in the evening rather than at bedtime — worth asking your prescriber about if it disrupts your sleep.

If a dose is missed, the standard rule applies: "if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the dose you missed and take your next dose when you are meant to"; otherwise take it as soon as remembered — never a double dose to make up for one missed [2].

Tell any doctor or anaesthetist you see about spironolactone before surgery, including day surgery — the leaflet specifically flags this as "especially important if you are going to receive an anaesthetic agent," because of its effect on fluid and electrolyte balance [2].
After an orchidectomy a blocker is no longer needed and is usually stopped [1].
sections.note: Spironolactone and potassium interact. Tell your pharmacist about any potassium supplements, salt substitutes or blood pressure medicines before you start [2][3].

body: Australian guidance describes 25 to 100 mg daily, and the position statement goes up to 200 mg daily [1][4].
list: Usual range — 25 to 100 mg daily [1][4]
Up to 200 mg daily in the Australian position statement [1]
Levels and bloods rechecked six to eight weeks after a change [1][4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Most of these are mild and often settle. Passing more urine is the effect people notice first.
list: Passing more urine, especially in the first weeks
Cramping or diarrhoea [2][3]
Nausea or vomiting [2][3]
Drowsiness, lethargy, or generally feeling unwell [2][3]
Rash, itch, peeling or reddened skin [2][3]
Unusual hair loss, or extra hair growth [2][3]
Breast or chest tenderness or growth [3]

body: The Spiractin leaflet says: "Call your doctor straight away, or go straight to the Emergency Department at your nearest hospital" for the serious effects below [2].

The one that matters most is potassium. Both leaflets warn that "too much potassium can cause serious problems, such as disturbances to the heart rhythm" [2][3]. Several common medicines raise that risk further if taken alongside spironolactone: ACE inhibitors and other potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen or indomethacin, and digoxin — tell your prescriber about any of these before starting [2].

Taking too much can cause "nausea and vomiting" and sometimes "drowsiness, mental confusion, rash, diarrhoea or dehydration" — contact the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) or go to the emergency department for a suspected overdose [2].
list: Palpitations, an irregular or slow heartbeat, or feeling faint — possible high potassium [2][3]
Muscle weakness, or numbness and tingling [3]
Chest pain [2]
Breathlessness with swelling of the legs [3]
Fever, severe chills, sore throat or mouth ulcers — possible blood problem [2][3]
Severe confusion, or bleeding from the stomach [3]
Rash with swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing [2]
sections.note: Do not take potassium supplements or use salt substitutes containing potassium while you are on spironolactone, and do not load up on potassium-rich foods like dried fruit, bananas and oranges without asking first [2][3]. If your heartbeat feels wrong, or you feel faint, call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department.

body: The specific extra checks for spironolactone are electrolytes — particularly potassium — and kidney function, along with your blood pressure [2][4].

The Spiractin leaflet describes the pattern: "Your doctor may do blood tests to check your sodium and potassium levels and see how your kidneys are working", potentially weekly at first, then monthly for three months, quarterly for a year, then every six months [2].
Alongside that, the usual feminising-therapy monitoring applies: trough oestradiol of about 250 to 600 pmol/L and total testosterone below 2 nmol/L in Australian guidance [1][4].
list: Potassium and sodium, and kidney function [2][4]
Blood pressure [2][4]
Oestradiol and total testosterone [1][4]
Weight at each review [1]

body: Spiractin: keep tablets "in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C", away from the bathroom, near a sink, the car and window sills [2].
Aldactone: "Keep Aldactone in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C" [3].
Keep out of reach of children, ideally in a locked cupboard well above floor level [2]. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Spironolactone is PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restrictions, so no authority is needed and the standard co-payment applies. The 25 mg tablet, 100 pack, is item 2339D [5].

Three brands share that item, and two of them carry a brand premium you pay on top of your co-payment. On the September 2026 listing, Spironolactone Viatris 25 had no premium, Spiractin 25 carried $4.42 and Aldactone carried $7.33 [5].

Brand premiums do not count towards the Safety Net and you still pay them after you have passed it. Ask your pharmacist for the benchmark brand if cost matters — swapping brands of the same medicine is routine.
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70; the yearly Safety Net thresholds are $1,748.20 general and $277.20 concessional [7].
A Section 19A approval for an overseas spironolactone product previously existed in Australia and has since lapsed [6].
A lapsed approval can mean the shortage resolved, or that the approval expired, so treat the current position as unconfirmed rather than assuming either way [6].
Because three brands are registered here, a shortage of one can usually be covered by another. Ask your pharmacist.

list: How often will my potassium and kidney function be checked, and what result would mean stopping or lowering the dose?
Are any of my other medicines — blood pressure tablets, painkillers, supplements — likely to raise my potassium further on top of this?
Would cyproterone suit me better, given my own health history?
If I need surgery or a general anaesthetic, does spironolactone need to be stopped or adjusted beforehand?
What symptoms of high potassium should I actually watch for day to day?
Is there a cheaper brand at my strength that avoids the premium I'm currently paying?

medicines.name: Testosterone undecanoate injection
medicines.forms: Deep intramuscular injection, 1,000 mg in 4 mL oily solution
medicines.summary: A long-acting testosterone injection given by a clinician every few months. It is the most widely used masculinising hormone in Australia, and the one that needs the fewest doses per year.

body: Testosterone undecanoate is testosterone in a slow-release oily form. Each vial contains 1,000 mg of testosterone undecanoate in 4 mL [2].
It is injected deep into muscle, and the testosterone is released slowly over the following months, which is why doses are ten to fourteen weeks apart rather than weekly or fortnightly [1][2].

Testosterone works by binding to androgen receptors throughout the body — muscle, skin, hair follicles, the voice box and the brain — driving masculinising changes as exposure continues. Menstrual suppression is usually the fastest visible change, "within 1–6 months," though periods can continue beyond 12 months in some people; most other effects begin within a few months but take two to three years to reach their maximum [1].

Several brands are now registered in Australia against the same PBS item, including Reandron 1000, Gonadron, Rejunon 1000 and Testosterone ADVZ 1000 [5]. They are the same medicine at the same strength.

High doses of testosterone can affect sperm production, and the manufacturer describes this as "reversible once treatment is stopped" — but ovulation and fertility do not reliably return quickly or predictably on their own, so oocyte or embryo storage is worth discussing with a prescriber before starting if that matters to you [1][2].
This is not a self-injection medicine in Australia. The leaflet says "the injection will be administered very slowly into your buttock muscle by your doctor" [2].

The slow injection is deliberate. Oily solutions can very rarely enter the bloodstream and reach the lungs, so the leaflet states: "The patient should therefore be observed during and immediately after each injection in order to allow for early recognition of possible signs and symptoms of pulmonary oily microembolism" [2].
Expect to be asked to stay at the clinic for a short period after the injection. That is standard practice for this medicine, not a sign anything is wrong.

Australian guidance describes a second dose about six weeks after the first, then a settled interval of ten to fourteen weeks [1][3]. The CMI does not give specific guidance for a late injection beyond stating the interval, so if you are going to run late, contact the clinic rather than guessing — they can advise whether to come in sooner or book the next available slot [2].

Taking more than prescribed does not speed up results; the leaflet notes that overdose is managed by "termination of therapy with the drug or dose reduction," and warning signs of too much include "irritability, nervousness, weight gain, or prolonged or frequent erections" [2].
sections.note: Book the next injection before you leave. Letting the interval stretch out is the commonest reason people get a dip in levels and a dip in how they feel.

body: 1,000 mg in 4 mL, given deep into muscle. A second dose about six weeks after the first, then one every ten to fourteen weeks [1][3][2].

The interval, rather than the amount, is what gets adjusted. If your trough level or your haematocrit is out of range, your prescriber is more likely to move the interval than change the volume [1][3].
list: 1,000 mg / 4 mL per dose, deep intramuscular [2]
Loading — second dose about six weeks after the first [1][3]
Maintenance — one dose every 10 to 14 weeks [1][2][3]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: The leaflet lists "weight gain, acne, enlarged prostate, hot flushes, injection site reactions" among the common effects [2].

Most of the changes people are actually seeking — voice deepening, body hair, redistribution of fat, periods stopping — are effects of testosterone rather than side effects, and they arrive over months to years, not weeks [1].
list: Soreness, ache or a lump at the injection site [2]
Acne, especially in the first year [2]
Weight gain [2]
Hot flushes [2]
Prostate enlargement, for people who have a prostate [2]
Mood changes
Increased body and facial hair, deepening voice, redistribution of fat and increased muscle mass, over months to years [1]
sections.note: Testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy and does not reliably stop ovulation. If pregnancy is possible for you, contraception is worth a specific conversation with your prescriber — do not assume testosterone covers it [1].

body: The leaflet flags "chest pains, sweating, signs of an allergic reaction, jaundice, prolonged painful erections, severe stomach pains or blood clots" as serious [2].

Two are specific to this injection. Pulmonary oily microembolism can cause "cough, dyspnoea, malaise, hyperhidrosis, chest pain, dizziness" during or just after the injection. Anaphylactic reactions have also been reported [2].

A few common medicines interact meaningfully with testosterone: it can increase the effect of warfarin-type anticoagulants, so a dose adjustment may be needed; combined with corticosteroids it can increase fluid retention; and it can improve glucose tolerance, sometimes reducing the insulin or other diabetes medicine dose needed [2]. Tell your prescriber about any of these before starting or changing dose.
list: Cough, sudden breathlessness, chest pain, sweating, feeling unwell or dizzy during or shortly after the injection — tell the clinician immediately, before you leave [2]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing [2]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2]
Severe abdominal pain [2]
Pain, heat or swelling in a leg, or sudden breathlessness later on — possible blood clot [2]
A prolonged or painful erection, for people who have erections [2]
sections.note: If any of these happen at the clinic, say so on the spot rather than waiting. If they happen at home, call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department. A prolonged painful erection is a medical emergency, not something to wait out.

body: The usual Australian target is a trough total testosterone of 10 to 15 nmol/L — measured at the lowest point, close to the end of the interval rather than soon after an injection [1][3][4].
Testosterone also thickens the blood, so haematocrit is checked on a full blood count. Above about 0.50 the dose or the interval is usually reviewed [1][3].
The leaflet adds that "your doctor may monitor your blood pressure, examine your prostate and conduct other tests from time to time" [2].
Screening still follows the organs you have. If you have a cervix, screening is still due every five years, and collecting your own swab is an option [1].
list: Trough total testosterone, timed near the end of the interval [1][3]
Haematocrit on a full blood count [1][3]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1][2]
Liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [1][3]
Reviews about every three months in the first year, then every six to twelve months [1]
sections.note: Ask for the required timing to be written on your pathology form, and tell the collection centre when your last injection was.

body: "Store it in a cool dry place away from moisture, heat or sunlight where the temperature stays below 30°C" [2].
In practice the clinic usually holds the vial, or you collect it from the pharmacy and bring it to the appointment on the day. If you are carrying it, keep it out of a hot car.
Sharps and used vials are disposed of by the clinic. Never put a needle in household rubbish.
PBS-listed, but Authority Required. The item is 10205D — testosterone undecanoate 1 g/4 mL modified release injection, 4 mL vial [5].
Your prescriber arranges the authority before you get to the pharmacy. Approval is usually immediate, by phone or online, and it is a funding step rather than a judgement about you.

The listed indications on the item are androgen deficiency, micropenis, pubertal induction, and constitutional delay of growth or puberty [5]. The Australian position statement tells prescribers to apply under androgen deficiency due to an established testicular disorder, with prescribing by or in consultation with a paediatrician, endocrinologist, urologist or sexual health physician whose name goes on the authority application [1].
If the authority is missing or expired, the pharmacy cannot charge you the PBS price. The fix is a phone call to your prescriber, not a private price — ask before you pay.
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][7].
sections.note: Every PBS testosterone item is listed for androgen deficiency and related conditions, not for gender affirmation, so the wording on the screen will not describe you. It is a quirk of a listing written before anyone was thinking about gender-affirming care, and it does not change your entitlement or your price.

body: No active TGA shortage record was found for testosterone undecanoate at last check [6].
Several brands now share the PBS item, which makes a total outage less likely: if one brand is unavailable, your pharmacist may be able to supply another at the same strength [5].

Because this medicine is given at a clinic rather than self-injected, running out usually means a scheduling problem rather than a stock problem — contact the clinic as soon as you know an appointment will be delayed, since letting the interval run past fourteen weeks lets your level fall before the next dose [1][3].

medicines.name: Testosterone enantate and testosterone esters
medicines.generic: Testosterone enantate (Primoteston Depot); mixed testosterone esters (Sustanon 250)
medicines.forms: Intramuscular injection. Primoteston Depot 250 mg/1 mL pre-filled syringe; Sustanon 250, 250 mg of mixed esters in 1 mL ampoule
medicines.summary: Shorter-acting testosterone injections given every two to four weeks. Both are registered in Australia but neither is PBS-subsidised, so they are private prescriptions.

body: These are shorter-acting testosterone injections. They clear faster than the long-acting undecanoate injection, so they are given more often and levels rise and fall more within each cycle. Testosterone works by binding to androgen receptors in muscle, skin, hair follicles, the voice box and the brain, driving masculinising changes over months to years as exposure continues [1].
Primoteston Depot contains "testosterone enantate" at 250 mg per 1 mL pre-filled syringe [2].

Sustanon 250 contains four esters mixed together: "testosterone propionate 30 mg, testosterone phenylpropionate 60 mg, testosterone isocaproate 60 mg, testosterone decanoate 100 mg" per 1 mL ampoule [3].
Because they peak and trough more, some people find the mood and energy swing more noticeable than on the long-acting injection. Others prefer the shorter interval because it is easier to adjust.

Both leaflets note that long-term or high-dose treatment can reduce sperm production, and describe this as reversible once treatment stops or the dose is lowered [2][3] — though in practice fertility does not always return quickly or predictably, so sperm cryopreservation is worth discussing with a prescriber before starting if that matters to you [1].

Both are given by injection into muscle by a health professional. Sustanon is injected deeply into the buttock, upper leg or arm [3]. Primoteston must be injected "extremely slowly" to reduce the risk of the oil reaching the bloodstream [2].

The leaflets describe different intervals from the ones used in gender-affirming care. Primoteston's leaflet gives one syringe every two to three weeks at first, then "every 3–4 weeks" for ongoing treatment adjusted to levels [2]. Sustanon's gives "one injection of SUSTANON '250' every 3 weeks" [3].

Australian gender-affirming practice generally uses 125 to 250 mg every two weeks [3][4][5]. If the interval you were given differs from the leaflet, that is expected — ask your prescriber why rather than changing it yourself.

If an injection is missed or delayed, Sustanon's leaflet is explicit: "talk to your doctor or nurse as soon as possible. No double dose should be injected to make up for forgotten individual doses" [3]. Primoteston's leaflet says to "keep your regular appointments to see the doctor" [2] — in practice, contact the clinic as soon as you know you will be late rather than waiting for the appointment date to pass.
Do not stop either medicine abruptly without medical advice: Primoteston's leaflet warns "do not stop using this medicine suddenly as you may experience withdrawal symptoms" [2].
sections.note: Sustanon contains arachis (peanut) oil: "Sustanon '250' is therefore contraindicated in patients allergic to peanuts or soya" [3]. It also contains benzyl alcohol. Tell your prescriber and pharmacist about any nut or soy allergy before your first dose.

body: Australian guidance describes 125 to 250 mg every two weeks for the shorter-acting esters in gender-affirming care [4][5].
list: Usual range in Australian guidance — 125 to 250 mg every two weeks [4][5]
Primoteston leaflet interval — every two to three weeks initially, then every three to four weeks [2]
Sustanon leaflet interval — one injection every three weeks [3]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Both leaflets report injection site pain, redness and swelling as common, along with acne, weight gain and changes in mood [2][3].
The masculinising changes themselves — voice deepening, body hair, fat redistribution, periods stopping — are the intended effects and take months to years [1].
list: Pain, redness or swelling where the injection went in [2][3]
Acne [2][3]
Weight gain [2][3]
Mood changes [2][3]
Muscle pain, or nausea [3]
Raised blood pressure [3]
Hair loss or thinning at the scalp [2][3]
Shrinkage of the testes, for people who have them [2][3]
sections.note: Testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy and does not reliably stop ovulation. If pregnancy is possible for you, contraception is worth a specific conversation with your prescriber — do not assume testosterone covers it [1].

body: Both leaflets treat the following as needing urgent care [2][3].

A small number of common medicines interact meaningfully with these injections: they can increase the effect of warfarin-type anticoagulants, so blood clotting times may need closer monitoring; combined with corticosteroids or ACTH they can increase fluid retention; and they can improve glucose tolerance, sometimes needing a lower insulin or diabetes medicine dose [2][3]. Mention any of these to your prescriber.

Chronic overdose can show up as polycythaemia (too many red blood cells) or priapism (a prolonged erection); both leaflets say the response is to stop treatment and, once symptoms settle, restart at a lower dose [2][3]. Contact the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) for advice on any suspected overdose.
list: Severe abdominal pain, or fainting [2]
Chest pain, or sudden breathlessness and cough during or just after the injection [2][3]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2][3]
"Unwanted, frequent or prolonged and painful erections" [2]
"Pain, swelling, redness, and enlarged veins in the affected area" — possible blood clot [3]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing — a severe allergic reaction, and a particular concern with Sustanon if you are allergic to peanuts or soya [3]
Marked mood disturbance [3]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for any of these. A prolonged painful erection needs treatment the same day.

body: The usual Australian target is a trough total testosterone of 10 to 15 nmol/L, plus haematocrit on a full blood count, with the dose or interval reviewed above about 0.50 [1][4][5].
With shorter-acting injections the timing of the sample matters especially: the trough is just before the next injection is due, not a few days after the last one [1][4].
list: Trough total testosterone, timed just before the next dose [1][4]
Haematocrit on a full blood count [1][4]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1][3]
Liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [1][4]
Cervical screening every five years if you have a cervix, with self-collection an option [1]

body: Primoteston Depot: store "below 25°C" in a cool dry place away from moisture, heat and sunlight, keeping the syringe in its original packaging until use [2].
Sustanon 250: "Keep it in a cool dark place where the temperature stays between below 30°C. Do not refrigerate as this makes the product difficult to inject" [3].
Keep both out of reach of children. Needles and syringes go into a sharps container, never household rubbish — your pharmacy or clinic can tell you where to get one and where to return it.
Neither is PBS-subsidised, so both are private prescriptions and you pay the pharmacy's full price [4].
Primoteston Depot was deleted from the PBS in February 2018 at the sponsor's request. Sustanon has never had a PBS listing [4].

Private prices vary between pharmacies and do not count towards the PBS Safety Net. It is entirely reasonable to ring around, and to ask your prescriber whether a PBS-subsidised alternative — the long-acting undecanoate injection, or a gel or cream — would suit you instead.
The TGA maintains a shortage record page for testosterone enantate, which is worth checking directly if your pharmacy cannot get Primoteston [6].
The TGA page for that product could not be read at the time of writing, so the current status here is unconfirmed rather than clear — ask your pharmacist, who can see the live position.

Because these are private prescriptions with no PBS-mandated brand, a pharmacist can usually substitute Primoteston for Sustanon or vice versa if one is unavailable — the underlying hormone is the same, though the release profile differs slightly, so check with your prescriber if the swap is more than a one-off.
