medicines.name: Testosterone gel
medicines.forms: Transdermal gel. Testogel 1% — 5 g sachets containing 50 mg, and a metered pump delivering 12.5 mg per press. Testavan 2% — metered pump with cap applicator delivering 23 mg per press
medicines.summary: A testosterone gel rubbed into the skin once a day. It suits people who prefer a daily routine, or who want the dose adjusted in small steps rather than every few months.

body: Testosterone gel delivers testosterone through the skin daily, instead of in one large dose every few months. Levels stay steadier day to day, and the dose can be moved in small increments. It works by binding to androgen receptors in muscle, skin, hair follicles, the voice box and the brain, driving masculinising changes over months to years [1].

Two products are registered in Australia at different concentrations. Testogel is 1%: a 5 g sachet contains 50 mg of testosterone, and the metered pump delivers 12.5 mg per press [2]. Testavan is 2%: the pump delivers 23 mg of testosterone per press, in 1.15 g of gel [3].
Because the concentrations differ, the number of pump presses is not transferable between the two. Never convert a Testogel dose into Testavan presses yourself.

Both leaflets note testosterone can reversibly suppress sperm production and shrink the testes over time [2][3] — though fertility does not always return quickly or predictably once stopped, so sperm cryopreservation is worth discussing with a prescriber before starting if that matters to you [1].
Once a day, on clean dry skin, at about the same time.

Testogel goes on the upper arms, shoulders or abdomen, and not on the genitals. Spread it as a thin layer without rubbing it in hard, allow three to five minutes to dry, then wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water [2].

Testavan goes on the upper arm and shoulder only, and comes with a cap applicator — you apply it with the applicator head rather than with your fingers. "Allow the gel to dry completely before getting dressed" and "wash hands well with soap and water after TESTAVAN has been applied" [3].
One practical warning specific to Testavan: "TESTAVAN is flammable until dry. Avoid fire, flame or smoking until the gel has dried" [3].

Showering timing affects how much is absorbed. Testogel's leaflet advises against showering or bathing "for at least one (1) hour after applying," and notes six hours is preferable [2]. For Testavan, research cited in the leaflet found showering one to two hours after application reduced absorption by 14 to 19%, while waiting six hours avoided that loss [3]. Sunscreen does not affect how Testogel works [2].
If a dose is missed, both leaflets give the same rule: "apply it as soon as you remember"; if it is already time for the next one, "just apply one dose" rather than doubling up [2][3].
list: Clean, dry, unbroken skin — approved sites only, never the genitals [2][3]
Let it dry fully, then cover the area with clothing [2][3]
Wash your hands with soap and water straight afterwards [2][3]
Use the applicator for Testavan rather than your hands [3]
No naked flames or smoking until Testavan has dried [3]
Wait one to six hours before showering, bathing or swimming where practical, to avoid washing off unabsorbed gel [2][3]
sections.note: Transfer is the main practical risk with gels. The Testogel leaflet's safety instruction is quoted here in its original wording: "Do not allow women (especially women that are pregnant or breast-feeding), children or pets to come into contact with the medicine or the skin where this medicine has been applied" [2]. Testavan puts it as: "TESTAVAN can transfer from your body to others. This can happen if other people come into contact with the area where TESTAVAN was applied" [3]. Covering the area with clothing once it is dry is the simplest way to prevent it.

body: Testogel: the leaflet's usual starting dose is one 5 g sachet daily (50 mg of testosterone), with a stated maximum of 10 g a day (100 mg) [2]. With the pump, Australian guidance describes typical use of one to four presses daily, each delivering 12.5 mg [4][5].
Testavan: the leaflet's starting dose is 23 mg daily — one press — with a maximum of 69 mg daily, or three presses [3].
list: Testogel sachets — one 5 g sachet (50 mg) daily to start, maximum 10 g daily [2]
Testogel pump — typically one to four presses daily, 12.5 mg per press [2][4][5]
Testavan — 23 mg (one press) daily to start, maximum 69 mg (three presses) [3]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Skin reactions where the gel goes on are the commonest effect specific to this form [2][3].
list: Skin irritation, redness or dryness at the application site [2][3]
Acne [2]
Headache or dizziness [2][3]
Mood changes or anxiety [2][3]
Raised blood pressure [2][3]
Hair loss or thinning at the scalp [2][3]
Easy bruising, or diarrhoea [3]
sections.note: Testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy and does not reliably stop ovulation. If pregnancy is possible for you, contraception is worth a specific conversation with your prescriber — do not assume testosterone covers it [1].

body: Both leaflets treat the following as needing urgent medical care [2][3].

A few common medicines interact meaningfully: warfarin-type anticoagulants may need closer monitoring of clotting times when gel is started or stopped; corticosteroids can increase fluid retention when combined with testosterone; and insulin or other diabetes medicines may need a lower dose as testosterone can improve glucose tolerance. Testavan's leaflet also lists bupropion and ciclosporin as interacting medicines [2][3].

If you think you or someone else has used too much, Testogel's leaflet says: "immediately telephone your doctor or the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for advice, or go to Accident and Emergency at the nearest hospital" [2]. For Testavan, the advice is to wash the skin with soap and water straight away, then seek the same advice [3].
list: Yellowing of the skin or eyes — liver problems [2][3]
Swelling or colour change in a leg, sudden breathlessness, coughing up blood, chest pain, severe dizziness or sudden vision loss — signs of a blood clot [2][3]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, rash, or trouble breathing — severe allergic reaction [3]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for any of these. Do not wait for an appointment. If someone else develops unexpected body hair, acne or voice changes after skin contact with you, that is not an emergency, but tell your prescriber — it means transfer is happening and the routine needs changing.

body: The usual Australian target is a trough total testosterone of 10 to 15 nmol/L, with haematocrit checked on a full blood count and the dose reviewed above about 0.50 [1][4].

Timing matters more for gel than for injections. The Equinox guide describes taking the sample in the morning before that day's dose, after at least a week of steady use [4]. A sample taken after you have applied the gel can read far too high.
list: Trough total testosterone, before the day's dose, after at least a week of steady use [1][4]
Haematocrit on a full blood count [1][4]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1][2]
Liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [1][4]
Cervical screening every five years if you have a cervix, with self-collection an option [1]
sections.note: Ask for the required timing to be written on your pathology form, and tell the collection centre when your last dose was.

body: Testogel: keep it below 25°C in a cool dry place, away from the bathroom, near a sink, window sills and the car [2].
Testavan: "Keep TESTAVAN in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C", in the original container, away from moisture and heat — and away from fire or flame until the gel has dried [3].
Keep gel well out of reach of children and pets, both because of the medicine and because of the transfer risk. Return what you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Both are PBS-listed, but Authority Required. Your prescriber arranges the authority before you get to the pharmacy — approval is usually immediate, by phone or online [6].

Testogel is listed as 1% (50 mg/5 g) gel, 30 x 5 g sachets (items 8830R and 13983Y) and as 1% (12.5 mg/actuation) gel, 2 x 60 actuations (items 10380H and 13924W). Testavan is listed as 2% (23 mg/actuation) gel, 56 actuations (items 11740X and 14025E) [6].
The listed indications on these items are androgen deficiency, micropenis, pubertal induction, and constitutional delay of growth or puberty [6].
If the authority is missing or has expired, the pharmacy cannot charge you the PBS price. The fix is a phone call to your prescriber, not a private price — ask before you pay.
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [6][8].

It is a quirk of a listing written before anyone was thinking about gender-affirming care, and it does not change your entitlement or your price.

medicines.name: Testosterone cream
medicines.forms: Transdermal cream. AndroForte 5 — 5% (50 mg/mL), 50 mL tube with measured applicator. AndroFeme 1 — 1% (10 mg/mL), tube with measured applicator
medicines.summary: A testosterone cream measured by the millilitre and rubbed into the skin daily. AndroForte 5 is the higher strength used in masculinising therapy; AndroFeme 1 is a much lower strength registered for a different purpose.

body: Cream works like gel — daily application through the skin, steadier levels than an injection, and a dose that can be moved in small steps. It is measured in millilitres using an applicator rather than in pump presses. Testosterone works by binding to androgen receptors in muscle, skin, hair follicles, the voice box and the brain, driving masculinising changes over months to years [1].
AndroForte 5 contains "50 mg testosterone per 1 mL of cream", made in Australia by Lawley Pharmaceuticals [2].

AndroFeme 1 is a much weaker cream: "10 mg testosterone per 1 mL of cream" [3]. It is registered in Australia for treating hypoactive sexual desire dysfunction after menopause, not for masculinising hormone therapy [3]. It is included here because people do encounter it, and because the tenfold difference in strength matters.
Never assume a millilitre of one is a millilitre of the other. They differ by a factor of ten.

AndroForte 5's leaflet notes that large doses of testosterone can suppress sperm production by reducing pituitary FSH, which can affect semen parameters including sperm count [2] — sperm cryopreservation is worth discussing with a prescriber before starting if that matters to you [1].
Once a day, measured with the applicator that comes with the tube, on clean dry skin.

AndroForte 5 has two approved application areas with different doses: the upper body — torso, abdomen and sides — or the entire scrotum. "Massage the cream into the area until absorbed. Typically, this takes 30 seconds or so", then "wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water after applying the cream" [2].

Timing around washing matters for absorption: "Do not shower or swim for at least six (6) hours after applying the cream to the upper body or two (2) hours after applying the cream to the scrotum" [2].
AndroFeme 1 is applied "directly onto clean, dry, healthy skin of either the upper outer thigh or buttock" [3].

If a dose is missed, both leaflets give the same instruction: "apply it as soon as you remember and continue to apply it as you would normally"; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one — never double up [2][3].
list: Measure the dose with the applicator, not by eye [2][3]
Massage in until absorbed, about 30 seconds [2]
Wash your hands with soap and water afterwards [2]
Cover the area with clothing once absorbed [3]
Do not shower or swim for six hours after an upper-body dose, or two hours after a scrotal dose [2]
sections.note: Both creams can transfer to other people through skin-to-skin contact. Keeping the area covered with clothing, and showering before close skin contact, are the practical steps the AndroFeme leaflet describes [3]. Do not let children or pets touch treated skin.

body: The Equinox prescribing guide describes typical use of 1 to 2 mL of 5% cream daily in gender-affirming care [4].

The AndroForte 5 leaflet's own starting doses are 2 mL applied to the upper body, with a maximum of 4 mL a day, or 0.5 mL applied to the scrotum, with a maximum of 1 mL a day — scrotal skin absorbs far more efficiently, which is why the scrotal dose is much smaller [2].

AndroFeme 1 is dosed quite differently for its registered purpose: "the usual starting dose is 0.5 mL (5 mg) of cream by measured applicator per day", with a maximum of 1.0 mL (10 mg) daily unless a doctor directs otherwise [3].
list: AndroForte 5, upper body — 2 mL daily to start, maximum 4 mL daily [2]
AndroForte 5, scrotal — 0.5 mL daily to start, maximum 1 mL daily [2]
Typical use described in Australian gender-affirming guidance — 1 to 2 mL of 5% cream daily [4]
AndroFeme 1 — 0.5 mL (5 mg) daily to start, maximum 1 mL (10 mg) daily [3]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Skin reactions at the application site are the effect specific to creams [2].
list: Skin irritation where the cream is applied [2]
Headache [2]
Mood changes [2]
Increased appetite and weight gain [2]
Changes in sex drive [2]
Acne, extra facial or body hair, and thinning of scalp hair [3]
sections.note: Testosterone can harm a developing pregnancy and does not reliably stop ovulation. If pregnancy is possible for you, contraception is worth a specific conversation with your prescriber — do not assume testosterone covers it [1].

body: Both leaflets treat the following as needing urgent care [2][3].

A few common medicines interact meaningfully with testosterone cream: warfarin-type anticoagulants may need closer INR monitoring, particularly when starting or stopping the cream; corticosteroids can increase fluid retention in combination; and insulin or other diabetes medicines may need a lower dose. AndroFeme 1's leaflet also flags bupropion, which can lower the seizure threshold in combination [2][3].

Taking too much is uncommon but the leaflets are clear: "if you think that you have used too much ANDROFEME 1, you may need urgent medical attention" — wash the skin with soap and water and contact the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) or go to the emergency department [2][3].
list: Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, rash, or trouble breathing — severe allergic reaction [2][3]
"Unwanted, frequent or prolonged and painful erections" for people who have erections [2]
"Numbness, heat or swelling in your arms or legs" — possible blood clot [2]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [3]
Swelling of the ankles with rapid weight gain [3]
Persistent headaches [3]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for an allergic reaction, a suspected clot, or a prolonged painful erection. Do not wait it out.

body: The usual Australian target is a trough total testosterone of 10 to 15 nmol/L, with haematocrit on a full blood count and the dose reviewed above about 0.50 [1][4].
As with gel, the sample is usually taken in the morning before that day's dose, after at least a week of steady use [4].
list: Trough total testosterone, before the day's dose [1][4]
Haematocrit on a full blood count [1][4]
Blood pressure and weight at each review [1]
Liver function and lipids as your prescriber decides [1][4]
Cervical screening every five years if you have a cervix, with self-collection an option [1]

body: AndroForte 5: "Keep ANDROFORTE 5 in a cool, dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C. Do not freeze", and use the tube within 125 days of opening it [2].
AndroFeme 1: "Store it in a cool dry place — below 25°C — away from moisture, heat or sunlight. Do not freeze", also with a 125-day in-use limit [3].

Write the date you opened the tube on it, since the in-use limit is shorter than the printed expiry. Keep both well out of reach of children and pets, and return what you no longer need to a pharmacy.
AndroForte 5 is PBS-listed, but Authority Required — testosterone 5% (50 mg/mL) cream, 50 mL, items 10378F and 14563L. Your prescriber arranges the authority before you get to the pharmacy [5].
The listed indications are androgen deficiency, micropenis, pubertal induction, and constitutional delay of growth or puberty [5].

AndroFeme 1 is registered in Australia but is not PBS-subsidised, so it is a private prescription and you pay the pharmacy's full price. The PBAC considered a submission for it in November 2025 and did not recommend listing [6].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 — this applies to AndroForte 5, not to the private AndroFeme 1 [5][8].
sections.note: Every PBS testosterone item is listed for androgen deficiency and related conditions, not for gender affirmation, so the wording on the screen will not describe you. It is a quirk of a listing written before anyone was thinking about gender-affirming care, and it does not change your entitlement or your price.

body: No active TGA shortage record was found for AndroForte 5 at last check, and no substitution instrument is in effect for it [7].
Both creams are made in Australia by Lawley Pharmaceuticals, which has historically meant fewer of the global supply problems that have affected imported patches [2][3].

medicines.name: GnRH analogues (puberty blockers)
medicines.forms: Zoladex — goserelin 3.6 mg subcutaneous implant, every 28 days. Lucrin Depot — leuprorelin powder for intramuscular injection, including 3.75 mg and 11.25 mg, and a 30 mg paediatric presentation given every three months. Eligard — leuprorelin subcutaneous injection, 7.5 mg monthly, 22.5 mg three-monthly, 30 mg four-monthly and 45 mg six-monthly
medicines.summary: Injections or implants that pause puberty by switching off the hormone signal from the brain. They are always used under specialist care, and in Australia they are not PBS-subsidised for puberty suppression.

body: GnRH analogues work upstream of the sex hormones. Instead of blocking testosterone or oestrogen where it acts, they switch off the signal from the brain that tells the gonads to make it at all.

The effect is a pause rather than a permanent change, which is why they are described as giving time — time before the physical changes of puberty go further, and time to make decisions [1]. The Zoladex leaflet describes the mechanism in two phases: an "initial stimulation of pituitary LH secretion and a transient elevation in serum testosterone" or oestradiol in the first days of treatment, followed by suppression of that same pituitary signal with ongoing use, reaching full hormone suppression within about three weeks [2].

That initial surge, sometimes called a flare, can briefly worsen symptoms the medicine is meant to control before it settles — Eligard's leaflet describes it as a "transient exacerbation of symptoms and signs" in the first days [4]. It is a known, expected part of starting treatment rather than a sign it is not working.

Two medicines are used in Australia. Goserelin (Zoladex) is "a very small pellet" implanted under the skin of the abdominal wall, given "every 28 days" [2]. Leuprorelin comes as Lucrin Depot, an intramuscular injection, and Eligard, a subcutaneous injection, at intervals from one to six months depending on the strength [3][4].
They are also sometimes used in adults as an adjunct to lower testosterone, not only for puberty suppression. Either way this is specialist prescribing.

Fertility is affected while the medicine is active — Zoladex's leaflet describes "profound impairment of fertility" during treatment, generally reversible once it is stopped [2]. Fertility preservation options are worth discussing with the specialist team before starting, particularly once puberty has progressed further than its earliest stages [1].
Always given by a health professional — there is no take-home version.
Zoladex 3.6 mg is injected under the skin of the abdominal wall using a SafeSystem syringe with a protective needle sleeve, and is repeated every 28 days [2].

Eligard is "injected underneath the skin" by a health professional, with the site rotated between doses [4]. Its strengths map to different intervals: 7.5 mg monthly, 22.5 mg every three months, 30 mg every four months and 45 mg every six months [4].
Lucrin Depot is given as an intramuscular injection. The paediatric 30 mg presentation, registered for central precocious puberty, is given "once every three months as a single injection" [3].

Keeping to the interval matters more here than with most medicines, because a late dose lets the paused signal restart. Zoladex's leaflet is explicit: "do not omit or delay injections, as serum testosterone or serum oestradiol levels may rise" if a dose is missed [2]. If an appointment cannot be kept, Eligard's leaflet says to "contact your doctor, nurse or pharmacist to find out what to do" rather than rebooking for whenever suits [4]. Book the next appointment before you leave.
Do not stop treatment without discussing it with the treating team first — both leaflets warn that hormone levels rise again once the medicine is stopped or missed for long enough [2][4].
In Australian gender-affirming care the medicines used are goserelin (Zoladex) or leuprorelin (Lucrin, Eligard), repeated every one to three months, always under specialist care [1].

The registered strengths and intervals are set by the product, not chosen freely: Zoladex 3.6 mg every 28 days [2]; Eligard 7.5 mg monthly, 22.5 mg three-monthly, 30 mg four-monthly, 45 mg six-monthly [4]; Lucrin Depot paediatric 30 mg every three months [3].
list: Goserelin (Zoladex) 3.6 mg implant, every 28 days [2]
Leuprorelin (Eligard) 7.5 mg monthly, or a longer-acting strength [4]
Leuprorelin (Lucrin Depot) intramuscular, including a 30 mg paediatric presentation every three months [3]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above are the ranges Australian guidance works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Most reported effects come from the drop in sex hormones rather than from the medicine itself, and settle within the roughly three weeks it takes for suppression to establish after each new course begins [2].
list: Hot flushes and sweating [2][3][4]
Reduced sex drive [2][4]
Pain, swelling, bruising or redness at the injection or implant site [2][3][4]
Headache [3][4]
Tiredness and dizziness [3][4]
Mood changes, including tearfulness [3]
Breast or chest tenderness [2]
Periods stopping, for people who have them [2]
A brief worsening of symptoms in the first days of a new course, before suppression takes hold (the "flare") [2][4]

body: The leaflets treat the following as needing urgent medical care [2][3][4].

Because GnRH analogues can affect heart rhythm, they interact with other medicines that carry the same risk — methadone, some antipsychotics and heart rhythm medicines including quinidine, disopyramide, amiodarone and sotalol — so tell the treating team about all other medicines being taken [4]. Oral contraceptives can also interfere with how well the medicine works [2].

Taking a dose early or a higher dose than intended has not been linked to clinically important harm in the data the leaflet cites, but any suspected overdose or unexpected reaction should still go to the Poisons Information Centre (13 11 26) or the nearest emergency department [2][4].
list: "Swelling of the face, lips, mouth, throat or neck which may cause difficulty in swallowing or breathing" [3]
Severe headache with loss of vision [2][4]
Chest pain, or difficulty breathing [2][4]
Symptoms of a stroke, or sudden tingling or numbness in the limbs, or collapse [4]
Severe abdominal pain, or signs of bleeding [2]
Weakness or numbness in the legs, difficulty passing urine, or new bone pain [2]
Unsteadiness when walking, or blood in the urine [3]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for any of these. A severe headache with vision loss needs same-day assessment, not a wait.

body: Bone health is the specific monitoring for this group, because blockers pause the bone strengthening that puberty normally provides [1].

The Zoladex leaflet is direct about the effect: "The use of Zoladex causes a loss of bone mineral density" [2]. The Lucrin paediatric leaflet notes that "bone loss (decreased bone mineral density) may occur during treatment" but that "after the treatment is stopped, bone loss is reversed" [3]. Eligard's leaflet says to "keep all of your appointments, including those for blood tests and bone density tests" [4].
Puberty stage, growth and hormone levels are also tracked over time by the treating specialist team [1].
list: Bone density, and bone health generally [1][2][3][4]
Height, weight and pubertal stage [1]
Hormone levels as the specialist team directs [4]
Mood and wellbeing at each review [1]

body: These are clinic-held medicines, so storage is usually the clinic's or pharmacy's job rather than yours.
Zoladex: keep "in a cool, dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C", away from the bathroom, sinks and direct sunlight [2].
Lucrin Depot paediatric: "kept in a cool, dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C, and should be protected from light" [3].

Eligard needs refrigeration below 8°C before it is dispensed, and after that "keep ELIGARD in a place where the temperature stays below 25°C for up to 8 weeks before injection" [4]. If you collect it from a pharmacy, ask how to transport it and how long you have.
Needles and used devices are disposed of by the clinic.

GnRH analogues are not PBS-subsidised for puberty suppression. That is the single biggest cost issue in this part of gender-affirming care. SA Health's model of care notes that a young person who cannot access them through a hospital faces a cost of several thousand dollars a year on a private prescription [5].

These medicines do have PBS listings for other conditions, which is why a pharmacist may see a subsidised price on screen for a different indication. That does not make the prescription you hold a PBS one — ask your prescriber directly whether yours is PBS or private.

Access to goserelin is changing. The PBS announced in July 2026 that the goserelin 3.6 mg implant (Zoladex) leaves the PBS on 1 November 2026, and that the sponsor has set up the Zoladex Continuity Program to keep supplying it at no cost to eligible patients, arranged through prescribers [6]. The medicine continues; the paperwork changes.
If this affects you or your child, raise it with your prescriber and your pharmacist well before the next dose is due, not in the week it falls due.
The goserelin change is a funding and access change, not a manufacturing shortage — worth keeping separate in your head, because the two are managed completely differently [6].
Only an older New Zealand notice turned up for leuprorelin, with nothing confirming a current Australian shortage. Treat that as no evidence of a shortage rather than a guaranteed all-clear [7].
Because these are clinic-supplied medicines, the clinic usually knows about a supply problem before you do. Ask at your next appointment if you are worried.

medicines.name: Doxycycline
medicines.forms: Oral tablet or capsule. 50 mg and 100 mg immediate-release tablets (several brands); Doryx is a 50 mg modified-release capsule
medicines.summary: An oral tetracycline antibiotic. In gender-affirming care it is the step up once topical treatment is not controlling acne that has become moderate to severe on testosterone.

body: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic. It slows bacterial growth, but at the low, long-course dose used for acne it is prescribed mainly for its anti-inflammatory effect on the skin — calming the redness and inflammation around blocked pores — rather than to clear an infection [2].

Testosterone increases oil (sebum) production in the skin, which is why acne is common in the first year or two of masculinising therapy [1]. Once topical treatment alone is not controlling it, the Australian practical guide on prescribing hormone therapy describes the escalation as "topical therapies, tetracyclines or referral for isotretinoin" [4], and the position statement notes that "moderate to severe acne may require oral antibiotics or isotretinoin" [1].

It is the same medicine used far more often for other things — chest infections, some sexually transmissible infections, and malaria prevention for travellers — so the leaflet that comes with it describes all of those uses, not just acne [2].
For acne, the usual course is a low daily dose for a set number of weeks, not an ongoing medicine — the Doxsig leaflet's acne dosing is "50 mg once daily" for "12 weeks" [2].

"Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass of water or milk while sitting or standing upright", and "do not lie down immediately after swallowing" — stay upright for at least half an hour, because the tablet can irritate or ulcerate the oesophagus if it sits against it [2].
Taking it with food reduces stomach upset. Leave a gap of at least two hours from iron tablets, antacids or calcium supplements, which reduce how much is absorbed [2].
If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless the next one is nearly due, in which case skip it — "do not take a double dose" [2].
list: 50 mg once daily for a set course, usually around 12 weeks, for acne [2]
Swallow whole with a full glass of water or milk [2]
Stay upright for at least 30 minutes after each dose [2]
Leave two hours either side of iron, antacids or calcium supplements [2]
sections.note: Doxycycline makes skin more sensitive to UV light — it "may cause your skin to become more sensitive to UV or sunlight, resulting in severe sunburn" — relevant to Australian sun exposure, and worth mentioning to your prescriber if you're also using a topical acne treatment that already dries or irritates the skin [2].

body: For acne specifically, 50 mg once daily is the dose described in the Australian leaflet, run for a defined course rather than continued indefinitely [2].
Higher doses — up to 200 mg daily — are used for the other infections doxycycline treats, but that is not the acne dose, and not what most people on testosterone are prescribed it for [2].
list: Acne — 50 mg once daily, typically for around 12 weeks [2]
Reviewed against how the skin responds, not against a blood level [1][4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose or course length. The figures above describe how doxycycline is generally used for acne, not a recommendation for you.

body: Most of these are mild, and the same regardless of why someone is taking it.
list: Oral or vaginal thrush [2]
Nausea, vomiting or stomach upset [2]
Loss of taste, or a metallic taste [2]
Ringing in the ears (tinnitus) [2]
Skin that burns or reddens more easily in the sun [2]

body: Chest pain or pain on swallowing after a dose can mean the tablet has irritated the oesophagus — taking it with plenty of water and staying upright helps prevent this, but tell your prescriber if it happens [2].

Doxycycline is not usually prescribed alongside isotretinoin, another acne treatment described on this site: combining a tetracycline with isotretinoin raises the risk of raised pressure around the brain (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) [2][3].
Doxycycline can make some contraceptive pills less reliable — worth flagging if you or a partner rely on one for contraception [2].
list: Persistent headache with visual disturbance — possible raised pressure around the brain [2]
Severe skin reaction, blistering or peeling [2]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or difficulty breathing — severe allergic reaction [2]
Severe or persistent diarrhoea [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for a severe allergic reaction or difficulty breathing. Do not wait for an appointment.

body: There is no blood test specific to doxycycline itself. What is actually tracked is the acne — whether it is settling over the weeks of the course [1][4].
It does not interfere with the testosterone or haematocrit blood tests used to monitor hormone therapy, so it can usually be taken alongside your usual testing schedule without changing the timing.
list: How the skin is responding, usually reviewed toward the end of the course [2][4]
Any new interacting medicine, including contraception or other acne treatments [2]

body: "Store below 30°C. Protect from light and moisture" [2].

Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need, including an unfinished course, to a pharmacy rather than keeping it — a later course needs a fresh prescription rather than leftover tablets.

Doxycycline is PBS-listed as a Restricted Benefit rather than unrestricted — the listed indications are bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis and severe acne, so your prescriber notes the acne indication on the script [5].
Brands and prices vary under the same item — on the listing checked, a modified-release brand and a standard generic were both available at different prices [5].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][7].
Doxycycline is a widely stocked generic antibiotic with several brands registered in Australia, which usually means one brand's shortage can be covered by another [6].

Australia has had nationwide shortages affecting some antibiotics in recent years; check with your pharmacist if your usual brand or pack size is unavailable, since a substitution between doxycycline brands is generally straightforward [6].

medicines.name: Topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide
medicines.generic: Adapalene, with or without benzoyl peroxide
medicines.forms: Topical gel. Epiduo — adapalene 0.1% and benzoyl peroxide 2.5%; Epiduo Forte — adapalene 0.3% and benzoyl peroxide 2.5%
medicines.summary: A once-daily gel combining a retinoid (a vitamin A derivative) with benzoyl peroxide. Usually the first treatment tried for acne that develops on testosterone, before anything taken by mouth.

body: Adapalene is a retinoid — it unblocks pores and reduces inflammation. Benzoyl peroxide adds an antibacterial, oil-reducing effect. Together they treat acne from two directions at once [2].

Testosterone increases oil (sebum) production in the skin, which is why acne is common in the first year or two of masculinising therapy [1]. The position statement describes this combination as the first-line topical option: "topical retinoids or retinoid–benzoyl peroxide combinations are useful for mild to moderate acne", with oral antibiotics or isotretinoin reserved for what topical treatment alone doesn't control [1].
Epiduo and Epiduo Forte are the same combination at two strengths — Epiduo Forte has three times the adapalene, for skin that hasn't responded well enough to the standard strength [2].

Once a day, on clean, dry skin. "Apply once a day, on a clean and dry skin", spreading "a thin film of gel evenly over the entire acne affected area(s)" — the face, chest or back, wherever acne occurs — rather than dabbing it on individual spots [2].
Avoid the eyes, lips and the inside of the nose, and wash your hands afterwards [2].
Dryness, peeling and mild burning are common in the first couple of weeks as the skin adjusts; a plain, fragrance-free moisturiser and staying out of strong sun help [2].
If a dose is missed, apply it at the next scheduled time — "do not apply a double dose to make up for forgotten individual doses" [2].
list: Once daily, thin layer over the whole acne-affected area, not just individual spots [2]
Clean, dry skin — avoid eyes, lips and the inside of the nose [2]
Wash your hands after applying [2]
Moisturise and limit sun exposure while your skin adjusts [2]
sections.note: Expect the first two to four weeks to feel worse before it gets better — dryness and mild irritation early on are common and usually settle rather than meaning the treatment isn't working [2].

body: One application, once a day, is the standard use for both strengths — there is no dose titration in the way there is for a hormone [2].
Australian guidance places this combination as the option to try first for mild to moderate testosterone-related acne, moving to an oral antibiotic or isotretinoin if it isn't enough [1][3].
list: Epiduo (0.1%/2.5%) or Epiduo Forte (0.3%/2.5%) — once daily [2]
Usually given a few months' trial before judging whether it's working [1]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can advise on which strength and how long to trial it.

body: Skin irritation, particularly in the first two to four weeks, is the effect specific to this treatment [2].
list: Dry skin [2]
Stinging or burning sensation on application [2]
Mild peeling or scaling [2]
Redness at the application site [2]

body: Genuine allergic reactions to a topical gel are uncommon, but the leaflet is clear about what to do if one happens [2].
Adapalene should not be used in pregnancy or while trying to conceive — relevant if pregnancy is possible for you, since testosterone does not reliably prevent it [1][2].
list: Swelling of the face, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing — severe allergic reaction [2]
Blistering or severe burning of the skin, well beyond the usual early irritation [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for a severe allergic reaction. "Do not use EPIDUO if you are pregnant or are planning a pregnancy" — tell your prescriber straight away if you find out you're pregnant while using it [2].

body: No blood test is needed for this treatment. What is tracked is whether the acne is improving, usually reviewed a couple of months into use [1][3].
list: How the skin is responding, reviewed at follow-up [1][3]
Whether irritation is settling or getting in the way of using it consistently [2]

body: "Keep EPIDUO in a cool, dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C. Do not refrigerate", and avoid the bathroom and direct sunlight [2].
Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Epiduo is PBS-listed as a Restricted Benefit for "severe acne vulgaris" as "acute treatment" — adapalene 0.1% / benzoyl peroxide 2.5% gel, 30 g, item 8954G [4].
Epiduo Forte's PBS status was not confirmed this session — ask your pharmacy whether the higher strength is subsidised on your script or needs to be paid privately.
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [4][5].

No current TGA shortage notice was located for Epiduo or Epiduo Forte in Australia. That is not the same as a confirmed all-clear, so check with your pharmacist if you're having trouble filling a script [6].

medicines.name: Isotretinoin
medicines.forms: Oral capsule. 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg and 40 mg (Oratane)
medicines.summary: A strong oral retinoid for acne that is severe, scarring, or has not responded to other treatment. Australian guidance points to it once testosterone-related acne needs a dermatologist.

body: Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative that shrinks the skin's oil glands and sharply reduces oil production and inflammation. A single course often clears severe acne for good, rather than needing to be repeated indefinitely like a topical treatment [2].

Australia's informed-consent guideline for masculinising hormone therapy lists "referral to dermatologist for isotretinoin" as a management option for acne alongside more standard measures, and the position statement puts it as the option for acne that oral antibiotics haven't controlled [1][3].
It is prescribed and monitored under strict rules because of serious risks, particularly in pregnancy, described below [2].
Dose is based on body weight and adjusted to response — typically "0.5 mg/kg bodyweight daily" to start, moving up to around 1 mg/kg/day — and it "must always be taken with food" [2].
Capsules are swallowed whole with a glass of water or milk. A course usually runs four to eight months [2].

Anyone who could become pregnant needs a negative pregnancy test before starting, effective contraception for a month before, during and a month after treatment, and treatment usually starts "on the second or third day of the next normal menstrual period" [2]. Testosterone does not reliably prevent ovulation, so this requirement applies to trans masculine people who could become pregnant just as it would to anyone else — worth an explicit conversation with your prescriber [1][2].
If a dose is missed, skip it and continue the regular schedule — "do not take a double dose to make up for the dose you missed" [2].
list: Dose set by bodyweight, always taken with food [2]
Course usually four to eight months [2]
Pregnancy test and effective contraception required beforehand if pregnancy is possible for you [2]
Regular blood tests through the course — see What is monitored below
sections.note: Isotretinoin is not usually combined with a tetracycline antibiotic like doxycycline — the combination raises the risk of raised pressure around the brain (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) [2].

body: The CMI's weight-based range — roughly 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily — is the standard Australian dosing, adjusted by your dermatologist through the course [2].
It sits at the far end of the acne treatment pathway Australian guidance describes: topical treatment, then an oral antibiotic, then isotretinoin if acne is severe or hasn't responded [1][3][4].
list: About 0.5 to 1 mg/kg bodyweight daily, taken with food [2]
Reviewed monthly through a four- to eight-month course [2]
sections.note: Only a dermatologist prescribing isotretinoin can set your dose and course length. The figures above describe the range Australian prescribing works within, not a recommendation for you.

body: Dryness is near-universal on isotretinoin and usually needs active management — lip balm, moisturiser and eye drops are worth having ready before you start.
list: Dryness of the lips, mouth, nose and skin [2]
Dry, sore, swollen or itchy eyes [2]
A temporary flare of acne in the first few weeks [2]
Joint or muscle aches [2]

body: Mood change is the effect taken most seriously. The leaflet lists "feeling depressed, with or without suicidal thoughts" as a reason to contact your prescriber — tell someone straight away if this happens, and tell your prescriber even if you're not sure it's related [2].

Isotretinoin can raise liver enzymes and blood fats (triglycerides and cholesterol), which is why these are checked through the course, and it has been linked to inflammatory bowel disease in rare cases [2].
list: Low mood, or thoughts of suicide or self-harm [2]
Persistent headache with visual disturbance [2]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2]
Severe abdominal pain, or blood in stools [2]
Severe skin reaction, blistering or peeling (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for a severe skin reaction or thoughts of self-harm needing immediate safety. Otherwise, contact your prescriber promptly — do not wait for the next scheduled review.

body: Isotretinoin needs more monitoring than most medicines on this site. Liver function is checked before starting and monthly through the course, alongside blood fats (triglycerides and cholesterol) [2].
Anyone who could become pregnant has monthly pregnancy tests through treatment [2]. Mood is checked in at each review, given the depression and suicidal-thoughts warning above.
list: Liver function tests — before starting, then monthly [2]
Triglycerides and cholesterol [2]
Pregnancy testing monthly if pregnancy is possible for you [2]
Mood, at every review [2]

body: Store "in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C" for most strengths, protected from light, and keep capsules in their blister pack until you take them [2].
Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Isotretinoin is PBS-listed, Authority Required (Streamlined), for "severe cystic acne" — for example, the 30 mg capsule, 60 pack, item 11921K [5].
The streamlined authority means your dermatologist can apply it directly on the script without a separate phone call, and up to three repeats can be written [5].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][7].

No current TGA shortage notice was located for Oratane in Australia. That is not the same as a confirmed all-clear, so ask your pharmacist ahead of time if you're worried about continuity through a course [6].

medicines.name: Norethisterone
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, 5 mg
medicines.summary: A progestogen tablet, at a higher dose than in a contraceptive pill, that stops or delays a period. Some people on testosterone take it to manage periods that have not settled.

body: Norethisterone is a progestogen. At the dose used here it works mainly by keeping the uterine lining from building up and shedding, which is what causes a period [2].

Testosterone alone often reduces or stops periods over time, but not reliably, and not always quickly — which is why some people add a second medicine specifically for menstrual suppression [1]. TransHub describes this directly: "a small amount of progesterone in combination with testosterone can help make sure you don't get a period" [3].

The Australian practical guide on prescribing puts a number on it: "a prescription of norethisterone 5 mg orally twice daily may provide temporary amenorrhoea and reduce distress" for someone whose periods are a source of dysphoria [4].
For ongoing suppression, norethisterone is generally taken continuously, at a dose and frequency your prescriber sets — the guide above describes 5 mg twice daily as an example [4].
The tablet "should be swallowed whole with a glass of water", and "it does not matter if you take the tablets before or after food" [2].

Norethisterone is also used, separately, to delay a period by a set number of days — a different, shorter regimen from the one used for ongoing suppression, so don't assume the two doses are interchangeable [2].
If a dose is missed: "only take the last missed tablet as soon as you remember and then continue taking your tablet at your usual time on the next day" [2].
list: 5 mg tablets, dose and frequency set by your prescriber for ongoing suppression [2][4]
Swallowed whole, with or without food [2]
Different, shorter regimen used if the goal is delaying a single period rather than ongoing suppression [2]
sections.note: Norethisterone at this dose is not necessarily reliable contraception on its own — ask your prescriber specifically about contraception if pregnancy is possible for you and matters to prevent [1].

body: 5 mg twice daily is the dose specifically described in Australian guidance for menstrual suppression associated with dysphoria [4].

The CMI's broader dosing range — 1 to 4 tablets daily depending on the condition being treated — reflects norethisterone's other uses (irregular bleeding, endometriosis, delaying a period) rather than this specific purpose [2].
list: Menstrual suppression — commonly 5 mg twice daily [4]
Adjusted by your prescriber against how well periods are controlled [2][4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. The figures above describe how norethisterone is generally used for this purpose, not a recommendation for you.

body: Breakthrough spotting is common, especially in the first months of continuous use, and doesn't necessarily mean it isn't working.
list: Nausea [2]
Headache, including migraines [2]
Fluid retention [2]
Breast or chest tenderness [2]
Mood changes [2]

body: Blood clots are the serious risk the leaflet focuses on, including "thrombophlebitis and pulmonary embolism" — tell your prescriber about any personal or family history of clots before starting [2].
A severe allergic reaction is described as "difficulty breathing, swollen tongue" and needs emergency care [2].
list: Swelling or pain in one leg, or sudden chest pain and breathlessness — possible blood clot [2]
Sudden, severe or unusual headache, or vision changes [2]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or difficulty breathing [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for a suspected blood clot or a severe allergic reaction. Do not wait for an appointment.

body: There's no blood test specific to norethisterone. What's tracked is whether it's actually achieving what you and your prescriber wanted — fewer or no periods — and whether bleeding, mood or other effects are tolerable [2][4].
list: Bleeding pattern, reviewed clinically [2][4]
Blood pressure at review [2]
Any new symptoms suggesting a clot risk, reported promptly rather than waiting for the next appointment

body: "Keep your tablets in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C" [2].
Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Norethisterone is PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restrictions — norethisterone 5 mg tablet, 30 pack, item 2993M, brand Primolut N [5].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][7].

No shortage notice specific to Primolut N was located this session. A related but different product — the combined oral contraceptives Brevinor and Norimin, which also contain norethisterone alongside an oestrogen — has had a confirmed TGA shortage notice; that is not the same medicine as Primolut N, so don't assume one implies the other [6].

medicines.name: Medroxyprogesterone acetate
medicines.forms: Deep intramuscular injection (Depo-Provera, 150 mg/mL) or oral tablet (Provera, 5 mg and 10 mg)
medicines.summary: A progestogen given as a three-monthly injection or as a tablet to stop periods; the injection also works as contraception. One of the options for menstrual suppression on testosterone.

body: Medroxyprogesterone acetate is a progestogen. Depo-Provera, the injectable form, suppresses ovulation and thins the uterine lining enough to stop periods for most people who use it continuously; Provera, the tablet, is used at various doses for period problems more broadly [2].

TransHub's page on contraception for trans people describes "contraceptive injections containing medroxyprogesterone" among the options that can also affect periods [3]. The position statement lists "oral progestins" as one option for periods that persist and cause distress on testosterone — medroxyprogesterone acetate is one of the progestins used this way [1].
The injectable and oral forms are dosed completely differently, so don't assume figures for one apply to the other.
Depo-Provera is given by a doctor or trained nurse, as "the recommended dose... for effective contraception" of "150 mg every three months", by deep injection into a muscle, usually the buttock [2].

If you run late for a repeat injection, that matters: "if the time between your injections is greater than 14 weeks, your doctor will need to check that you are not pregnant before they give you another injection" [2].
Provera tablets are taken by mouth at a dose your prescriber sets for the specific reason you're using it — this is a different regimen from the injection, not an oral version of the same dose.
list: Depo-Provera — 150 mg by injection every 12 weeks, given by a clinician [2]
More than 14 weeks between injections means a pregnancy check before the next one [2]
Provera tablets — dose set by your prescriber for the reason you're taking it [2]
sections.note: Depo-Provera is not something you can be a few weeks late for without it mattering — book your next injection before the 12-week mark, not after.

body: 150 mg every three months is the standard Australian dose for Depo-Provera used for contraception and period suppression together [2].

Many people using it purely for menstrual suppression while on testosterone use the injectable form for convenience — one appointment every twelve weeks rather than a daily tablet — but that is a preference to discuss with your prescriber, not a rule [1][3].
list: Depo-Provera — 150 mg every 12 weeks [2]
Provera tablets — dose individualised [2]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose or schedule.

body: Changed periods are the most common effect: "most women using DEPO-PROVERA for contraception experience changes in their normal monthly period", including irregular bleeding at first and, for most people, no periods at all with continued use [2].
list: Irregular bleeding or spotting, especially in the first few months [2]
No periods at all with continued use, for most people [2]
Weight gain — an average of 3.68 kg over two years was recorded in the leaflet's own data [2]
Headache, or mood changes [2]

body: The specific warning for Depo-Provera is bone density: "use of Depo-Provera reduces serum estrogen levels and is associated with a statistically significant loss of BMD [bone mineral density]", which matters more the longer it's used and especially if it's started young, before peak bone density is reached [2]. This is worth an explicit conversation if you're also not on oestrogen from another source and plan to use it for a long period.
list: Persistent bone or joint pain, worth raising at review rather than waiting [2]
Swelling or pain in one leg, or sudden chest pain and breathlessness — possible blood clot [2]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or difficulty breathing — severe allergic reaction [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for a suspected blood clot or a severe allergic reaction. Ask your prescriber directly about the bone density warning if you expect to use this for more than a couple of years.

body: There's no routine blood test specific to medroxyprogesterone acetate. What's tracked clinically is your bleeding pattern, weight, and — for longer-term use — bone health, which your prescriber may want to revisit periodically given the leaflet's own bone density warning [2].
list: Bleeding pattern, reviewed at follow-up [2]
Weight [2]
Bone health considerations for continued long-term use [2]

body: "Keep DEPO-PROVERA in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 30°C. Do not keep it in the refrigerator or freezer" [2].
Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Depo-Provera is PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restrictions — medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg/mL injection, 1 mL pre-filled syringe, item 14160G [4].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [4][6].

No current TGA shortage notice was located for Depo-Provera in Australia. That is not the same as a confirmed all-clear, so check with your pharmacy or clinic ahead of a repeat injection if you're concerned [5].

medicines.name: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device
medicines.forms: Intrauterine device, 52 mg levonorgestrel, releasing about 20 micrograms per day initially, fitted by a clinician
medicines.summary: A small hormone-releasing device fitted inside the uterus that stops or lightens periods and provides long-acting contraception at the same time. For menstrual suppression on testosterone, it avoids a daily tablet or a repeat appointment every few months.

body: Mirena releases a progestogen, levonorgestrel, directly inside the uterus. The dose that reaches the rest of the body is much lower than with a tablet or injection, because most of it acts locally to thin the uterine lining [2].

The position statement lists "progestin-releasing intrauterine devices" as an option for periods that persist and cause distress on testosterone [1]. TransHub's contraception page names "hormonal IUDs (like Mirena)" among the options available to trans people, alongside the reminder that "testosterone alone is not an effective form of contraception for people with a uterus" [3].
Because it's fitted once and then left in place, it suits people who'd rather not manage a daily tablet or a repeat injection every twelve weeks.
A doctor or nurse fits it inside the uterus during a clinic procedure, ideally "within seven days from the beginning of your period" [2]. It is not something you manage day to day once it's in.

"After each menstrual period check that the device is in place by feeling for the thin threads attached to the lower end" — if periods stop altogether, which is common with continued use, this check is less relevant [2].
Wait roughly 48 hours after insertion before penetrative vaginal intercourse [2].
list: Fitted by a clinician, typically within a week of your period starting [2]
Lasts up to 8 years for contraception, 5 years for heavy bleeding [2]
Check the threads after each period, if you're still having them [2]
sections.note: Insertion itself can be uncomfortable, and testosterone can thin vaginal and cervical tissue over time — it's worth asking your clinician what pain relief or local anaesthetic options are available before the appointment, rather than on the day.

body: There's no dose to adjust in the way there is for a tablet or injection — it's a single device, replaced only when its registered duration runs out [2].
list: One device, fitted once [2]
Up to 8 years for contraception; up to 5 years for heavy menstrual bleeding [2]
sections.note: Your prescriber will advise which duration applies to why you're using it.

body: Irregular bleeding in the first few months is the effect almost everyone notices, and it usually settles: "you may have frequent spotting or light bleeding in addition to your periods for the first 3-6 months" [2].
list: Spotting or irregular bleeding for the first three to six months [2]
Tender breasts or chest [2]
Mood changes [2]
Headache [2]

body: The device can occasionally come out partially or fully (expulsion) without you noticing straight away, which is what the thread checks are for [2]. Perforation of the uterus at insertion is rare [2].
list: Excessive abdominal pain [2]
Fever, chills or generally feeling unwell — possible pelvic infection [2]
Heavy or unusual vaginal bleeding [2]
Cannot feel the threads, or they feel longer or shorter than usual — possible expulsion or movement of the device [2]
sections.note: Seek prompt medical attention for "excessive abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding, fever, chills or generally feeling unwell" [2]. This is not usually a 000 emergency, but shouldn't wait for a routine appointment either.

body: There's no blood test involved. A follow-up visit a few weeks after fitting checks the threads and that everything is settling as expected, and after that it's mainly about noticing any of the symptoms above [2].
list: Thread position, checked at follow-up and then by you periodically [2]
Bleeding pattern over the following months [2]

body: The device itself is stored by the clinic until it's fitted. If you're given the sealed pack to bring to your appointment, "store it in a cool dry place away from moisture, heat or sunlight where the temperature stays below 30°C" until then [2].
Removal, like fitting, needs a clinician — don't attempt to remove it yourself.
Mirena is PBS-listed — levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine drug delivery system, item 8633J — supplied through a medical or nurse practitioner rather than picked up like an ordinary script [4].

The device itself is subsidised on the PBS, but the insertion procedure is usually billed separately by the clinic or through Medicare, so ask about the total cost of the appointment, not just the device [4].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [4][6].

No device-specific TGA shortage notice was located for Mirena this session. Access has been discussed more broadly in Australian media in terms of appointment availability and cost of insertion rather than a stock shortage of the device itself — ask your clinic about wait times for fitting [5].

list: What pain relief or local anaesthetic options are available for fitting, given testosterone can make vaginal tissue more sensitive?
How soon might my periods lighten or stop after insertion, and what's normal in the meantime?
Who do I see for removal if I want it out before the registered duration is up, and is that covered?
Does this affect my testosterone dose or monitoring in any way?

medicines.name: Vaginal oestrogen
medicines.forms: Vaginal pessary (tablet), 10 micrograms estradiol, inserted with an applicator
medicines.summary: A very low, local dose of oestrogen inserted into the vagina, with little reaching the rest of the body. Treats the dryness and irritation testosterone can cause in vaginal tissue over time.

body: Testosterone lowers circulating oestrogen, and over time that can thin and dry vaginal tissue in a way similar to menopause — sometimes causing irritation, dryness or pain with penetration. Vaginal oestrogen treats that tissue directly, at a dose small enough that very little reaches the rest of the body [2].

Australia's hormone therapy prescribing guide puts it plainly: "for vaginal irritation / atrophy clients can use Vagifem low, twice weekly if desired" [3]. The practical prescribing guide describes the same approach: "a twice-weekly 10 µg vaginal oestradiol pessary may be acceptable to the patient and will often reduce symptoms" [4]. The informed-consent guideline lists "topical oestrogen" alongside vaginal moisturisers as options for this specific side effect of testosterone [1].

This is a different medicine, used a different way, from the estradiol tablets, patches and gels used in feminising therapy — the dose here is a fraction of a systemic dose, and it isn't intended to feminise or to counteract masculinising changes elsewhere in the body.
Inserted into the vagina with the applicator provided, as deep as is comfortable [2].
The usual pattern is "one Vagifem Low pessary each day for the first two weeks, then one pessary twice a week", spaced three to four days apart [2].
If a dose is missed, insert it as soon as you remember — "do not use a double dose to make up for the dose you missed" [2].
list: Daily for the first two weeks, then twice weekly, three to four days apart [2]
Inserted with the applicator provided [2]
Ongoing use, for as long as symptoms need it [1][3]
sections.note: This does not need to be timed around your testosterone dose, and it is not expected to change your testosterone level or your masculinising progress — ask your prescriber directly if you're worried about this.

body: Twice weekly, after an initial two-week daily loading period, is the pattern described both in the product's own leaflet and in Australian gender-affirming guidance [2][3][4].
list: Loading: one pessary daily for two weeks [2]
Maintenance: one pessary twice a week [2][3][4]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can advise on how long to continue, and whether the dose needs adjusting.

body: Local effects at the site are what's most likely, rather than anything felt elsewhere in the body given how small the dose is.
list: Vaginal thrush [2]
Vaginal discharge or spotting, particularly when starting [2]
Itching or a genital rash [2]
Headache [2]

body: Because a little oestrogen does reach the bloodstream, the same warning signs that apply to systemic oestrogen are listed on the leaflet, even though the risk is much lower at this dose [2].
list: Sudden chest pain and difficulty breathing [2]
Severe pain or swelling in a leg [2]
Unexplained vaginal bleeding beyond spotting [2]
A new, migraine-type headache [2]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for sudden chest pain, breathlessness or a suspected blood clot. Tell your prescriber promptly about unexplained bleeding or a new migraine-type headache rather than waiting for your next review.

body: Given how little reaches the bloodstream, routine blood tests aren't usually needed for this alone — review is mostly about whether the dryness or irritation has actually improved [1][2].
list: Symptom response, reviewed clinically [1][3][4]
Any bleeding pattern that doesn't fit the expected early spotting [2]

body: "Store below 25°C. Store in a dry place protected from light. Do not refrigerate" [2].
Keep out of reach of children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Vagifem Low is PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restrictions — estradiol 10 microgram modified-release pessary, 18 pack, item 10203B, shared with the brand Estro-Pess [5].
The PBS general patient co-payment is currently $25.00 per script, and the concessional co-payment is $7.70 [5][6].

No shortage notice specific to Vagifem Low was located this session. This is a separate product from the estradiol patches affected by Australia's long-running HRT patch shortage, so that shortage doesn't directly apply here — but check with your pharmacist if you're having trouble filling a script [7].

medicines.name: Finasteride
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, 1 mg (for hair loss — a separate 5 mg strength is used for an unrelated prostate condition)
medicines.summary: A tablet that blocks the conversion of testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in the scalp. An emerging option for androgenic hair loss in people on testosterone, and occasionally used in feminising care as well.

body: Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor: it blocks the enzyme that converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the form most responsible for shrinking scalp hair follicles in androgenic (pattern) hair loss [2].

Testosterone therapy can bring on or worsen this pattern of scalp thinning over time. Australia's 2026 standards of care note the evidence specifically in trans men: "a small retrospective case review found that low-dose finasteride in trans men resulted in modest improvements in hair loss, with no reports of sexual side effects" [1]. The same document flags that the sexual side effects seen with this drug class in cisgender men — "the use of 5ARI in cis men has been associated with sexual side effects, depression and suicidal thoughts" — haven't been reported in that small trans-specific study, though the evidence base is still limited [1].

It works differently from spironolactone or cyproterone, the anti-androgens used in feminising therapy on this site — finasteride targets one specific enzyme in hair follicles rather than blocking androgen receptors more broadly.
"The dose is one tablet taken once each day", with or without food [2].
Results take time — the leaflet describes at least three months of daily use before any change is likely to be visible, and continued use is needed to keep any benefit [2].
If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember, then continue your normal schedule — don't double up [2].
list: One 1 mg tablet daily, with or without food [2]
At least three months before results are likely to be noticeable [2]
Ongoing use needed to maintain any benefit — stopping generally reverses the effect over months
sections.note: The tablets must not be handled by anyone who is or might be pregnant if the tablets are crushed or broken — finasteride absorbed through the skin this way can affect a male fetus. Whole, uncrushed tablets are not a risk to handle normally [2].

body: 1 mg once daily is the standard Australian dose for hair loss, the same as the case review referenced in the Australian standards of care used [1][2].

This is a different strength from the 5 mg finasteride tablet used for an unrelated prostate condition — they are not interchangeable, and 1 mg products are specifically registered and marketed for hair loss [2].
list: 1 mg once daily [1][2]
Reviewed by how hair loss is tracking over months, not by a blood test [1]
sections.note: Only your prescriber can advise whether finasteride is appropriate for you and at what dose. The evidence specific to people taking testosterone is still limited to a small case review [1].

body: The evidence specific to people taking testosterone on testosterone is limited, but the effects described here come from the wider evidence base for this medicine.
list: Reduced libido or difficulty with erections, for people who have erections [2]
Breast or chest tenderness or enlargement [2]
Skin rash [2]

body: Sexual side effects are the ones most reported with this medicine, and the leaflet specifically flags that they can persist: "difficulty achieving an erection or less desire for sex, that continues after stopping" [2]. Tell your prescriber if this happens rather than assuming it will resolve on its own.
Mood effects are taken seriously: depression and suicidal thoughts are listed as effects reported after this medicine reached the market, and need prompt attention [2].
list: Low mood, or thoughts of self-harm [2]
Sexual side effects that persist or don't improve [2]
Breast or chest lumps, pain or discharge [2]
Swelling of the face, lips, mouth or throat, or difficulty breathing — severe allergic reaction [2]
sections.note: Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department for a severe allergic reaction, or if you're in immediate danger from thoughts of self-harm. Otherwise, raise mood or sexual side effects with your prescriber rather than stopping quietly — there may be other options.

body: There's no blood test specific to finasteride for hair loss. If you also have a prostate (relevant mainly in feminising care, where finasteride is sometimes used alongside other anti-androgens), it's worth knowing finasteride lowers PSA levels by roughly half, which can throw off prostate screening interpretation if that's ever relevant to you — mention you're taking it to whoever orders that test [2].
list: Hair loss progress, tracked by photos or clinical review over months [1]
Mood and sexual side effects, checked in on at review [2]
PSA test results interpreted with finasteride in mind, if relevant to you [2]

body: "Keep Finasteride GH 1 in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C" [2].
Keep out of reach of children and anyone who is or might be pregnant. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Finasteride 1 mg for hair loss is not PBS-subsidised in Australia — the only PBS listing for finasteride is the unrelated 5 mg strength, Authority Required, for benign prostatic hyperplasia [3].

This means a private script and the pharmacy's own price for the 1 mg strength, which varies considerably between brands — generic finasteride 1 mg is usually cheaper than the original Propecia brand.

Several brands of 1 mg finasteride are registered in Australia, which generally means good availability even if one particular brand is temporarily out of stock — ask your pharmacist about a generic alternative rather than assuming a shortage [4].

How will we track whether it's actually working, and over what timeframe?
What should I do if I notice sexual side effects or a change in mood?

medicines.name: Topical minoxidil
medicines.forms: Topical solution or foam, 2% or 5%, applied to the scalp
medicines.summary: A pharmacy medicine applied to the scalp to encourage regrowth, without acting on testosterone or DHT. A non-hormonal option for hair thinning, used by some people on testosterone and, separately, sometimes considered in feminising care.

body: Minoxidil widens blood vessels in the scalp and appears to extend the growth phase of hair follicles, though exactly how it works isn't fully settled. Unlike finasteride, it doesn't act on testosterone or DHT directly [2].

Australia's 2026 standards of care list "topical and oral minoxidil" among the "non-hormonal treatment options" for hair loss, alongside things like low-level laser therapy and platelet-rich plasma, for people on either testosterone-based or oestradiol-based hormone therapy [1]. This page covers the topical form, which has a standard Australian consumer leaflet; oral minoxidil for hair loss is a low, off-label dose of a tablet otherwise used for blood pressure, usually compounded rather than sold as a standard product, and isn't covered here in the same detail.
It is bought over the counter at a pharmacy rather than needing a prescription.
Applied directly to a dry scalp, "up to half a capful" (for the foam) massaged gently into the area of hair loss, twice a day — morning and night [2].

Wash your hands after applying, and allow the product to stay in contact with the scalp for several hours before washing it out — the leaflet advises "at least 4 hours" before the scalp is washed again [2].
list: Twice daily, morning and night, to a dry scalp [2]
Up to half a capful of foam per application, massaged in [2]
Leave at least four hours before washing the scalp [2]
Wash your hands after applying [2]
sections.note: "An increase in hair shedding may occur within the first 2-6 weeks" of starting — this is usually a normal part of the hair cycle resetting, not a sign it's failing, but it can be alarming if you don't expect it [2].

body: The 5% strength ("extra strength") is the more commonly used concentration; a lower 2% strength also exists, sold under brands such as Women's Regaine [2].
It generally takes "at least four months" of consistent twice-daily use before any cosmetically noticeable regrowth appears — an important thing to know before judging whether it's working [2].
list: Twice daily — there is no dose to titrate beyond the strength (2% or 5%) you start with [2]
At least four months before results are likely to be visible [2]
sections.note: Ask your pharmacist or prescriber which strength suits you, particularly if you're also using other topical treatments on the same area.

body: Most side effects are local, at the site it's applied.
list: Itching and other skin irritation of the scalp [2]
Redness of the scalp [2]
Dry skin or scalp flaking [2]
Unwanted hair growth on other parts of the body it has spread to, such as the face, if it isn't washed off hands properly [2]

body: Minoxidil affects blood vessels, and though the amount absorbed through the skin is small, the leaflet lists cardiac symptoms as a reason to stop and seek advice [2].
list: Chest, arm or shoulder pain [2]
Rapid heartbeat [2]
A drop in blood pressure, or feeling faint [2]
Swelling or puffiness, particularly of the hands, feet or face [2]
Shortness of breath [2]
sections.note: Stop using it and seek medical advice for any of the above. This isn't usually a 000 emergency on its own, but chest pain or breathlessness that's new or severe should be assessed urgently.

body: There's no blood test for topical minoxidil. What matters is whether hair loss is stabilising or reversing, judged over months rather than weeks, and whether the scalp is tolerating it [1][2].
list: Hair regrowth, usually judged by photos over several months [2]
Scalp irritation, and whether it's manageable enough to keep using consistently [2]

body: Keep below 25°C, away from heat and open flame — the foam and solution are flammable until dry [2].
Store safely away from children. Return anything you no longer need to a pharmacy.
Topical minoxidil is a pharmacy medicine, not a prescription item, and is not PBS-subsidised — you pay the pharmacy's own price, which varies by brand and strength.
As an over-the-counter pharmacy product with several brands and strengths on Australian shelves, minoxidil is generally easy to source, and no TGA shortage notice was located for it this session [3].
