medicines.name: Estalis and Estalis Sequi (combined estradiol and norethisterone patches)
medicines.forms: Transdermal patch, changed twice weekly. Estalis Continuous 50/140 and 50/250 (the same combined patch worn continuously); Estalis Sequi 50/140 and 50/250 (a two-phase composite pack — an oestrogen-only patch for the first two weeks of each four-week cycle, then a combined estradiol + norethisterone acetate patch for the second two weeks)
medicines.summary: A patch that combines two hormones in one product — estradiol (an oestrogen) and norethisterone acetate (a progestogen) — changed twice a week. It is registered in Australia for menopausal hormone therapy in someone with a uterus, not for gender-affirming care, and the Australian position statement on transgender hormone therapy does not recommend routinely adding a progestogen to feminising treatment. This entry is background for someone who has already been prescribed it — it is not an argument against your prescriber's choice.

body: Estalis and Estalis Sequi are brand names for a patch that delivers two hormones through the skin at once — estradiol, an oestrogen, and norethisterone acetate, a progestogen (a synthetic hormone related to progesterone) [2][3].

Both are registered in Australia for menopausal hormone therapy in someone who still has a uterus (womb). The progestogen's job in that setting is to stop the uterine lining (endometrium) building up unopposed under oestrogen, which over years can lead to overgrowth of the lining (endometrial hyperplasia) or cancer. An oestrogen-only patch like Estradot doesn't carry that particular risk for someone without a uterus, which is most people using a patch for feminising hormone therapy [2][3].

That's the key thing to know if you've been given this rather than a plain oestrogen patch: it is doing a job — protecting a uterus — that most people on feminising hormone therapy don't need done. The Australian position statement on the hormonal management of transgender and gender diverse adults is direct about the progestogen component itself: "despite anecdotal reports that progestins increase breast growth, no data support their use." It lists thrombosis (blood clots), bloating, nausea and weight gain as added risks and concludes that progestins "are not recommended" in feminising therapy [1].

None of that means the patch was prescribed in error. There are a few genuine reasons someone might end up on a combined patch instead of a plain oestrogen one. During the long-running shortage of oestrogen-only patches (Estradot and Estraderm MX), some pharmacists and prescribers used a combined patch as one of the few transdermal oestrogen options actually on the shelf, accepting the extra progestogen as a trade-off for staying on a patch rather than switching to tablets or gel. Some prescribers who are more used to writing for menopausal hormone therapy may reach for a familiar combined product out of habit, without separately weighing whether the progestogen is doing anything for that particular patient. And a small number of people — for instance some intersex or non-binary people who do have a uterus — may genuinely need the endometrial protection this product provides [1][2][3]. Worth raising with whoever prescribed it, rather than assuming either that it's wrong or that it's necessary.

Two versions exist. Estalis Continuous delivers the same combined dose of both hormones every day, with no scheduled bleed. Estalis Sequi delivers oestrogen alone for the first two weeks of each four-week cycle, then adds the progestogen for the second two weeks — a pattern designed to produce a monthly withdrawal bleed, the way a natural cycle does [2][3].
list: Estalis Continuous 50/140 and 50/250 — combined estradiol + norethisterone acetate patch, worn continuously [2]
Estalis Sequi 50/140 and 50/250 — oestrogen-only patch for two weeks, then combined patch for two weeks, in a four-week composite pack [3]

body: Both products are changed twice a week, worn continuously for three or four days at a time [2][3].
Estalis Continuous uses the same combined patch every time, so there is nothing to sequence — just keep to your two weekly change days [2].

Estalis Sequi comes as a composite pack with two patch types in it. The oestrogen-only patches go on first, for the first two weeks of the four-week cycle, then the combined patches take over for the remaining two weeks. The pack is laid out in that order, and a calendar or diary helps keep track of which phase you're in [3].

Apply to a clean, dry area below the waist — commonly the lower abdomen or buttock — and rotate the site each time rather than reusing the same patch of skin. The patch must not be cut or trimmed, since that changes how much hormone is released [2][3].
list: Clean, dry, unbroken skin below the waist [2][3]
Rotate the application site every change [2][3]
Do not cut, trim or fold the patch to adjust the dose [2][3]
Keep it out of direct sunlight, a solarium, and very hot water or saunas where possible [2][3]
sections.note: If a patch falls off early, reapply it or apply a new one straight away and keep your usual two weekly change days — don't reset the schedule from the day it fell off [2][3].

body: Both Estalis Continuous and Estalis Sequi are available in two strengths — 50/140 (estradiol 50 micrograms/24h with norethisterone acetate 140 micrograms/24h) and 50/250 (estradiol 50 micrograms/24h with norethisterone acetate 250 micrograms/24h) [2][3].

There is no separate feminising-hormone-therapy dosing guidance for this combined product — the Australian position statement and prescribing guides describe dosing for oestrogen alone, not for a fixed oestrogen-plus-progestogen combination [1]. Whatever dose you're on will follow menopausal-therapy prescribing conventions rather than a transfeminine dosing schedule, which is worth knowing when comparing notes with dosing information written for plain oestrogen patches.
sections.note: Only your prescriber can set or change your dose. Don't double up patches or switch strengths to try to match a target you've read about for oestrogen-only therapy without checking first.

body: Most of the list below overlaps with any oestrogen patch, but irregular or unscheduled bleeding, breast tenderness and mood change are specifically tied to the progestogen component and are not things a plain oestrogen-only patch like Estradot typically causes [2][3].
list: Breast or chest tenderness [2][3]
Irregular vaginal-type bleeding or spotting — expected as a withdrawal bleed on Estalis Sequi, but worth mentioning if it happens on Estalis Continuous, where it isn't expected to be cyclical [2][3]
Nausea, abdominal cramping [2][3]
Headache [2][3]
Mood changes [2][3]
Fluid retention or swelling, weight gain [2][3]
Skin irritation at the patch site, vaginal irritation [2][3]

body: As with any oestrogen or progestogen product, the serious warnings are mostly about blood clots, stroke, the liver and allergic reactions.
list: Sudden shortness of breath, coughing up blood, chest pain — possible clot in the lung [2][3]
Unusual pain, heat or swelling in an arm or leg — possible clot in a vein [2][3]
Sudden severe headache, sudden loss of coordination, or blurred vision — possible stroke [2][3]
Severe abdominal pain with fever [2][3]
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice) [2][3]
Rash, swelling of the face, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing — possible allergic reaction [2][3]
sections.note: Do not wait for a GP appointment for chest pain, breathing difficulty, stroke symptoms or a severe allergic reaction. Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department.

body: The check-up schedule in the CMI is written for menopausal hormone therapy — at least once a year, covering breast checks and mammograms, and blood pressure [2][3].

That schedule doesn't automatically include the oestradiol and testosterone blood levels that feminising hormone therapy is usually tracked against [1]. If you're being monitored the way anyone on this site's other oestrogen products would be, it's worth confirming that explicitly rather than assuming it's included by default.
Store patches in a cool, dry place — not the bathroom, the car, or a window sill [2][3].

Fold a used patch in half with the sticky side inward before throwing it away, since a used patch still contains active hormone. Keep patches out of reach of children and pets, and ask your pharmacist about returning unused or unwanted patches [2][3].

All four Estalis products — Continuous 50/140, Continuous 50/250, Sequi 50/140 and Sequi 50/250 — are PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restriction, so any prescriber can write them and no authority is needed [4].

You pay the standard PBS co-payment — currently $25.00 per script for general patients, $7.70 for concession card holders — and scripts count toward the PBS Safety Net thresholds ($1,748.20 general, $277.20 concessional) for the calendar year [5].

The TGA's page on the transdermal HRT patch shortages lists all four Estalis products — Continuous 50/140, Continuous 50/250, Sequi 50/140 and Sequi 50/250 — as resolved, with no current shortage recorded [6].

That's a change since April 2025, when Estalis Continuous had been reported as limited and an overseas alternative was PBS-listed under a special arrangement. Worth double-checking with your pharmacy if your last experience of this product was during that period.

The separate Serious Scarcity Substitution Instrument that lets a pharmacist substitute between oestrogen-only patch brands (Estradot and Estraderm MX) does not cover this combined product — it applies only to oestrogen-only transdermal patches, not to anything containing norethisterone acetate [6].

medicines.name: Kliogest and Kliovance (combined estradiol and norethisterone tablets)
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, one per day from a 28-day calendar dial pack, taken continuously with no break between packs. Kliogest — estradiol 2 mg + norethisterone acetate 1 mg per tablet. Kliovance — a lower-dose version, estradiol 1 mg + norethisterone acetate 0.5 mg per tablet
medicines.summary: A tablet that combines two hormones in one pill — estradiol (an oestrogen) and norethisterone acetate (a progestogen) — taken once a day with no tablet-free break. It is registered in Australia for menopausal hormone therapy in someone with a uterus, not for gender-affirming care, and Australian guidance on feminising hormone therapy does not recommend routinely adding a progestogen. This entry is background for someone who has already been prescribed it — it is not an argument against your prescriber's choice.

body: Kliogest and Kliovance, both made by Novo Nordisk, are the same combination — estradiol, an oestrogen, plus norethisterone acetate, a progestogen (a synthetic hormone related to progesterone) — at two different strengths, taken as one tablet a day with no break [2][3].

Like all the combined products on this page, they're registered for menopausal hormone therapy in someone who still has a uterus, where the progestogen's job is to stop the uterine lining (endometrium) building up unopposed under oestrogen. That protective role isn't relevant for most people on feminising hormone therapy, who don't have a uterus [2][3].

The Australian position statement on transgender and gender diverse hormone management is explicit that adding a progestogen isn't supported by evidence for feminising goals like breast growth, and that it adds risk: "despite anecdotal reports that progestins increase breast growth, no data support their use," and progestins "can also increase risk of thrombosis, bloating, nausea and weight gain and are not recommended" [1].

If you've been prescribed this, a common reason is that a prescriber more used to menopausal hormone therapy defaulted to a familiar combined product rather than an oestrogen-only one, sometimes hoping the progestogen would add to breast development — a rationale the position statement specifically says isn't backed by evidence [1]. It's a reasonable thing to raise at your next appointment, alongside whether an oestrogen-only tablet like Progynova would do the same job with one less hormone on board.
Both come in a calendar dial dispenser. "Take one tablet a day, preferably at the same time each day, until all 28 tablets have been taken," then start the next pack immediately with no gap [2].

The dial is turned once a day, after the tablet for that day has been removed, so the pack itself tracks which day you're on. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless the next one is due soon, in which case skip it and continue the normal schedule rather than doubling up [2].

Kliogest is the higher-strength version (estradiol 2 mg + norethisterone acetate 1 mg); Kliovance is a lower-strength version of the same combination (estradiol 1 mg + norethisterone acetate 0.5 mg) [2][3].

As with the other products on this page, there's no feminising-hormone-therapy-specific dosing guidance for this combination — the Australian position statement and prescribing guides describe oestrogen-alone dosing, not a fixed combined product [1]. Whatever strength you're on will have been chosen against menopausal-therapy conventions, not a transfeminine target range.
The CMI describes these as usually settling with time: "these side effects are usually temporary and disappear" [2].
list: Breast changes — tenderness, pain, enlargement [2]
Irregular bleeding or heavier-than-usual bleeding [2]
Nausea, indigestion, bloating, diarrhoea [2]
Headache, migraine, dizziness [2]
Sleep disturbance, mood changes [2]
Fluid retention and swelling, weight fluctuation [2]
Vaginal fungal infection, hair or skin changes, leg cramps, back pain, visual disturbance [2]

body: The CMI separates an immediate-emergency list from a set of symptoms that mean the medicine should be stopped and reviewed.
list: Skin rash over a large part of the body, wheezing, swelling of the face, lips or tongue, a fast pulse, or sweating — possible severe allergic reaction [2]
Severe leg pain or swelling, unexplained chest pain, sudden difficulty breathing — possible blood clot [2]
Jaundice (yellowing of skin or eyes) [2]
Sudden severe or new-onset migraine-type headache, sudden vision problems [2]
A marked rise in blood pressure [2]
A new breast lump or skin dimpling [2]
sections.note: Do not wait for a GP appointment for chest pain, breathing difficulty, stroke symptoms or a severe allergic reaction. Call 000 or go to the nearest emergency department.

body: The CMI's schedule is annual: "once you have started on Kliogest you should see your doctor for regular check-ups (at least once a year)" to discuss benefits and risks of continuing, plus breast screening as recommended [2].

That's a menopausal-therapy monitoring schedule, not a feminising-hormone-therapy one — it doesn't automatically include oestradiol and testosterone blood levels the way this site's other oestrogen products are monitored [1]. Ask explicitly whether those are being tracked if that's what you're expecting.

"Keep Kliogest in a cool dry place where the temperature stays below 25°C. Do not put Kliogest in the refrigerator" — the same applies to Kliovance. Keep the pack in its outer carton for light protection, out of reach of children, and return unused tablets to a pharmacy [2].

Neither Kliogest nor Kliovance is PBS-subsidised — both are private prescriptions. A February 2026 report on menopausal hormone therapies left off the PBS listed Kliogest and Kliovance at around $47 each [4].
As private scripts, the price isn't fixed and can vary between pharmacies, and — unlike a PBS-subsidised item — the cost doesn't count toward the PBS Safety Net threshold.

No current TGA shortage notice was found for either Kliogest or Kliovance at the time of writing. Check the TGA's shortage database directly, or with your pharmacy, before assuming continued supply [5].

medicines.name: Trisequens (sequential estradiol and norethisterone tablets)
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, one per day from a 28-day calendar dial pack, taken continuously with no break between packs. Three tablet colours in sequence — blue (estradiol 2 mg alone, days 1 to 12), white (estradiol 2 mg + norethisterone acetate 1 mg, days 13 to 22), red (estradiol 1 mg alone, days 23 to 28)
medicines.summary: A tablet pack that cycles through three combinations of two hormones — estradiol (an oestrogen) alone, then estradiol with norethisterone acetate (a progestogen) added, then estradiol alone again — designed to produce a monthly bleed. It is registered in Australia for menopausal hormone therapy in someone with a uterus, not for gender-affirming care, and Australian guidance on feminising hormone therapy does not recommend routinely adding a progestogen. This entry is background for someone who has already been prescribed it — it is not an argument against your prescriber's choice.

body: Trisequens is a single product that changes composition through the pack. For twelve days it's estradiol alone; for ten days norethisterone acetate, a progestogen (a synthetic hormone related to progesterone), is added; then it drops back to estradiol alone for the last six days — a pattern built to mimic a natural cycle and trigger a withdrawal bleed toward the end of each pack [2].

It's registered for menopausal hormone therapy in someone who still has a uterus (womb), where the progestogen phase protects the uterine lining (endometrium) from building up unopposed under oestrogen. That protective role isn't relevant for most people on feminising hormone therapy, who don't have a uterus [2].

The Australian position statement on transgender and gender diverse hormone management doesn't support routinely adding a progestogen for feminising goals: "despite anecdotal reports that progestins increase breast growth, no data support their use," and progestins "can also increase risk of thrombosis, bloating, nausea and weight gain and are not recommended" [1].

Unlike the continuous combined products on this page (Kliogest, Femoston-Conti, Angeliq), Trisequens is specifically built to produce a scheduled monthly bleed. If you've been prescribed it, that's worth asking about directly — a bleed is the expected, designed-in effect of the progestogen phase here, not a side effect to worry about, but it's also a clear sign the product is doing something a plain oestrogen tablet wouldn't do.
One tablet a day from the dial pack, in the colour order the pack is set out in — blue, then white, then red — with the next pack started immediately with no gap [2].

The dial turns once a day after that day's tablet is removed, so the dispenser itself tracks where you are in the cycle. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless the next one is due soon, in which case skip it rather than doubling up [2].
sections.note: A bleed is expected toward the end of the white/red phase of each pack. Bleeding at other points in the cycle, or a bleed that's unusually heavy or prolonged, is worth mentioning to your prescriber rather than assuming it's routine [2].

body: Trisequens is registered in Australia in this single three-tablet configuration — there is no separate lower-dose version marketed here [2].

As with the other products on this page, there's no feminising-hormone-therapy-specific dosing target for this combination — Australian position-statement and prescribing guidance describes oestrogen-alone dosing, not a triphasic combined product [1].

Irregular spotting outside the expected withdrawal bleed [2]

Sudden severe headache, vision changes, slurred speech or numbness in a limb — possible stroke [2]

Severe abdominal pain with fever [2]

That doesn't automatically include the oestradiol and testosterone blood levels feminising hormone therapy is usually tracked against [1]. Confirm explicitly whether those are being monitored if that's what you expect.
Store in a cool, dry place, in the original dial pack, out of reach of children. Return any unused tablets to a pharmacy rather than putting them in household waste [2].
Trisequens is not PBS-subsidised — it's a private prescription. A February 2026 report on menopausal hormone therapies left off the PBS listed Trisequens at around $42 [3].
As a private script, the price can vary between pharmacies, and it doesn't count toward the PBS Safety Net threshold.
No current TGA shortage notice was found for Trisequens at the time of writing. Check the TGA's shortage database directly, or with your pharmacy, before assuming continued supply [4].

medicines.name: Femoston and Femoston-Conti (combined estradiol and dydrogesterone tablets)
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, one per day, taken continuously with no break. Femoston 1/10 and 2/10 are sequential packs of 28 — 14 oestrogen-only tablets followed by 14 tablets combining estradiol with dydrogesterone (a progestogen), at either the 1 mg or 2 mg estradiol strength. Femoston-Conti is a single continuous-combined tablet (estradiol 1 mg + dydrogesterone 5 mg) taken every day with no phases
medicines.summary: A tablet that combines two hormones — estradiol (an oestrogen) and dydrogesterone (a progestogen) — either in a sequential pack that produces a monthly bleed, or in a single continuous tablet that doesn't. It is registered in Australia for menopausal hormone therapy in someone with a uterus, not for gender-affirming care, and Australian guidance on feminising hormone therapy does not recommend routinely adding a progestogen. This entry is background for someone who has already been prescribed it — it is not an argument against your prescriber's choice.

body: Femoston products combine estradiol, an oestrogen, with dydrogesterone, a progestogen (a synthetic hormone related to progesterone). Femoston 1/10 and 2/10 are sequential — oestrogen alone for two weeks, then oestrogen plus dydrogesterone for two weeks. Femoston-Conti is continuous — the same combined tablet every day, with no phases and no scheduled bleed [2][3].

All three are registered for menopausal hormone therapy in someone who still has a uterus (womb), where the dydrogesterone protects the uterine lining (endometrium) from building up unopposed under oestrogen. That protective role isn't relevant for most people on feminising hormone therapy, who don't have a uterus [2][3].

The Australian position statement on transgender and gender diverse hormone management doesn't support routinely adding a progestogen for feminising goals: "despite anecdotal reports that progestins increase breast growth, no data support their use," and progestins "can also increase risk of thrombosis, bloating, nausea and weight gain and are not recommended" [1].

If you've been prescribed one of these, the most common reason is a menopausal-therapy prescribing default rather than a transfeminine-specific decision — worth raising directly, alongside whether an oestrogen-only tablet like Progynova, already covered elsewhere on this site, would meet the same goal.
Femoston 1/10 and 2/10: one tablet a day, taken in pack order — the white (oestrogen-only) section first, then the grey (combined) section — with the next pack started immediately and no gap [2].
Femoston-Conti: one tablet a day from a single pack, at roughly the same time each day, with the next pack started immediately after the last tablet [3].
sections.note: A withdrawal-type bleed is expected during or after the combined phase of Femoston 1/10 or 2/10. Femoston-Conti isn't designed to produce a scheduled bleed, so unexpected bleeding on it is worth mentioning to your prescriber [2][3].

body: Femoston 1/10 — estradiol 1 mg tablets, then estradiol 1 mg + dydrogesterone 10 mg tablets. Femoston 2/10 — estradiol 2 mg tablets, then estradiol 2 mg + dydrogesterone 10 mg tablets. Femoston-Conti — estradiol 1 mg + dydrogesterone 5 mg continuously [2][3].

As with the other products on this page, there's no feminising-hormone-therapy-specific dosing target for these combinations — Australian position-statement and prescribing guidance describes oestrogen-alone dosing [1].

body: Both CMIs describe an annual check-up — breast checks and mammograms, cervical screening, blood pressure and cholesterol, plus monthly self-checks — alongside general advice on calcium, vitamin D and exercise [2][3].

That's a menopausal-therapy monitoring schedule and doesn't automatically include the oestradiol and testosterone blood levels feminising hormone therapy is usually tracked against [1]. Confirm explicitly whether those are being monitored if that's what you expect.
Keep tablets in the original pack until you take them, stored below 30°C, away from bathrooms, cars and direct sunlight, and out of reach of children. Return unused tablets to a pharmacy [2][3].

Femoston 1/10 and Femoston 2/10 — the sequential packs — are PBS-listed on the General Schedule with no restriction, so any prescriber can write them and no authority is needed; you pay the standard co-payment [4].

Femoston-Conti — the continuous tablet — is not PBS-subsidised. A February 2026 report on menopausal hormone therapies left off the PBS listed it at around $15 as a private script [5]. This is a genuine practical difference: if cost is a factor, which regimen you're on changes what you pay, and it's worth asking whether the sequential and continuous versions could achieve the same thing for you.

No current TGA shortage notice was found for Femoston 1/10, 2/10 or Femoston-Conti at the time of writing. Check the TGA's shortage database directly, or with your pharmacy, before assuming continued supply [6].

medicines.name: Angeliq (combined estradiol and drospirenone tablets)
medicines.forms: Oral tablet, one per day, taken continuously with no break. Angeliq 1/2 — estradiol 1 mg + drospirenone 2 mg per tablet
medicines.summary: A tablet that combines two hormones — estradiol (an oestrogen) and drospirenone (a progestogen with its own mild diuretic-like effect) — taken once a day with no tablet-free break. It is registered in Australia for menopausal hormone therapy in someone with a uterus, not for gender-affirming care, and Australian guidance on feminising hormone therapy does not recommend routinely adding a progestogen. This entry is background for someone who has already been prescribed it — it is not an argument against your prescriber's choice — but the drospirenone component specifically is worth flagging with a pharmacist if you also take spironolactone.

body: Angeliq combines estradiol, an oestrogen, with drospirenone, a progestogen chemically related to spironolactone — the anti-androgen some people on feminising hormone therapy already take — and, like spironolactone, drospirenone has a mild fluid-shedding (antimineralocorticoid) effect that can raise blood potassium [2].

It's registered for menopausal hormone therapy in someone who still has a uterus (womb), where the drospirenone protects the uterine lining (endometrium) from building up unopposed under oestrogen. That protective role isn't relevant for most people on feminising hormone therapy, who don't have a uterus [2].

The Australian position statement on transgender and gender diverse hormone management doesn't support routinely adding a progestogen for feminising goals: "despite anecdotal reports that progestins increase breast growth, no data support their use," and progestins "can also increase risk of thrombosis, bloating, nausea and weight gain and are not recommended" [1].

There's an extra, practical reason to flag this specific product with a pharmacist: drospirenone's potassium-raising effect stacks with other medicines that do the same thing. Spironolactone falls into that category — the interaction is rated moderate, with drug-interaction references noting that "the use of drospirenone may potentiate the risk of hyperkalemia [high blood potassium] in patients receiving chronic treatment with drugs that can increase serum potassium such as... potassium-sparing diuretics, aldosterone antagonists," and recommending that "serum potassium levels should be checked regularly during concomitant therapy" [3]. If you're on both Angeliq and spironolactone, that's worth raising rather than assuming someone has already checked.
One tablet a day, at about the same time each day, swallowed whole with water. It isn't tied to meals, and the next pack starts immediately with no break [2].
Angeliq is registered in Australia as a single strength — labelled "1/2" for estradiol 1 mg and drospirenone 2 mg per tablet [2].

As with the other products on this page, there's no feminising-hormone-therapy-specific dosing target for this combination — Australian position-statement and prescribing guidance describes oestrogen-alone dosing [1].

Breast pain — described as very common in early treatment [2]
Nausea, abdominal pain, bloating [2]

Sudden shortness of breath, leg swelling or pain, coughing blood — possible blood clot [2]
Chest pain, symptoms of stroke [2]

Muscle weakness, an irregular heartbeat, or tingling — possible signs of high blood potassium (hyperkalaemia), particularly if you're also taking spironolactone, an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker, or another potassium-sparing medicine [3]

That doesn't automatically include the oestradiol and testosterone blood levels feminising hormone therapy is usually tracked against [1], and it doesn't automatically include a potassium check either. If you're also on spironolactone or another potassium-raising medicine, ask specifically whether blood potassium is being checked — drug-interaction guidance for drospirenone recommends checking it after around two weeks of combined use and periodically after that [3].
Store below 30°C in a cool, dry place, away from bathrooms and direct sunlight, out of reach of children. Return unused tablets to a pharmacy [2].
Angeliq is not PBS-subsidised — it's a private prescription. A February 2026 report on menopausal hormone therapies left off the PBS listed Angeliq 1/2 at around $52 [4].
As a private script, the price can vary between pharmacies, and it doesn't count toward the PBS Safety Net threshold.
No current TGA shortage notice was found for Angeliq at the time of writing. Check the TGA's shortage database directly, or with your pharmacy, before assuming continued supply [5].
